items.title: google-deepmind/mujoco
items.content:
Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact. A general purpose physics simulator.

stands for lti-int dynamics with ntact. It is a general purpose physics engine that aims to facilitate research and development in robotics, biomechanics, graphics and animation, machine learning, and other areas which demand fast and accurate simulation of articulated structures interacting with their environment.

MuJoCo has a C API and is intended for researchers and developers. The runtime simulation module is tuned to maximize performance and operates on low-level data structures that are preallocated by the built-in XML compiler. The library includes interactive visualization in native desktop windows and web browsers. MuJoCo further exposes a large number of utility functions for computing physics-related quantities.

MuJoCo's documentation can be found at mujoco.readthedocs.io. Upcoming features due for the next release can be found in the changelog in the "latest" branch.

  1. Try MuJoCo in your browser. Visit mujoco.org to explore MuJoCo on desktop or mobile with nothing to install, or open live.mujoco.org to inspect and drag and drop your own models in the WebAssembly version of the MuJoCo Studio app (slower than native C, since it runs in WebAssembly).

  2. Run a viewer on your machine. Follow the Getting Started guide in the documentation to download a prebuilt release and run the MuJoCo Studio app or the classic viewer (shown in this video) on your machine.

  3. Explore our online IPython notebooks. If you are a Python user, you might want to start with our tutorial notebooks running on Google Colab:

Versioned releases are available as precompiled binaries from the GitHub releases page, built for Linux (x86-64 and AArch64), Windows (x86-64 only), and macOS (universal). This is the recommended way to use the software.

Users who wish to build MuJoCo from source should consult the build from source section of the documentation. However, note that the commit at the tip of the branch may be unstable.

The native Python bindings, which come pre-packaged with a copy of MuJoCo, can be installed from PyPI via:

Note that Pre-built Linux wheels target , see here for compatible distributions. For more information such as building the bindings from source, see the Python bindings section of the documentation.

We aim to release MuJoCo in the first week of each month. Our versioning standards changed to modified Semantic Versioning in 3.5.0, see versioning for details.

We welcome community engagement: questions, requests for help, bug reports and feature requests. To read more about bug reports, feature requests and more ambitious contributions, please see our contributors guide and style guide.

Bug reports and feature requests

GitHub Issues are reserved for bug reports, feature requests and other development-related subjects.

MuJoCo is the backbone for numerous environment packages. Below we list several bindings and converters.

These packages give users of various languages access to MuJoCo functionality:

  • : gz-mujoco is a two-way SDFormat <-> MJCF conversion tool.
  • : obj2mjcf a script for converting composite OBJ files into a loadable MJCF model.

If you use MuJoCo for published research, please cite:

@inproceedings{todorov2012mujoco,
  title={MuJoCo: A physics engine for model-based control},
  author={Todorov, Emanuel and Erez, Tom and Tassa, Yuval},
  booktitle={2012 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems},
  pages={5026--5033},
  year={2012},
  organization={IEEE},
  doi={10.1109/IROS.2012.6386109}
}

items.content:
NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE). A management plane for GPU Kubernetes on bare metal.

Run a managed Kubernetes service on your own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure. NVIDIA Kubernetes® Engine (NVKE) provides the management plane that platform teams install to create and operate Kubernetes clusters for their customers. Each workload cluster has its own Kubernetes control plane, etcd and node pools. You operate the NVKE management plane; your customers use their clusters through the Kubernetes API and .

NVKE is available as a preview. APIs, configuration and behavior can change between releases, and we do not recommend NVKE for production workloads. See Preview status and known limitations.

Evaluate without GPU hardwareA development management plane and a workload cluster on simulated machines. No NVIDIA account is required.
Install on your infrastructureThe prerequisites and sequence for preparing nodes, bootstrapping a management cluster and installing its services.
The NVKE binaries and the contributor development loop.

The local quickstart runs on a Linux host or VM, amd64 or arm64, with at least 6 CPUs, 12 GiB of free memory and 100 GiB of free disk. It requires Docker, virtual TPM support and the tools listed in the guide. Follow its setup through workload-cluster creation and confirm the cluster's nodes report . On macOS, use the local site guide, which runs the evaluation inside a Colima virtual machine.

For a real installation, you supply the machines, networking, node images and registries, and configure access to NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo). NICo is the sole compatible infrastructure provider at preview. The platform and version reference lists validated combinations and pinned dependencies.

  • Creates independent workload clusters. Request clusters through the NVKE API or ; NVKE provisions machines through NICo and forms Kubernetes clusters with their own control planes.
  • Manages workload cluster lifecycle. Create, scale and delete node pools, upgrade Kubernetes and replace nodes. See the node pool guide for the manual steps and preview limits on replacement and upgrades.
  • Establishes node identity. Nodes attest through SPIFFE/SPIRE using their TPM before receiving join credentials. Encryption of etcd data is available per cluster.
  • Connects builds to deployment. Its companion project, NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR), builds node images and NVKE components from pinned inputs. NVKE deploys those artifacts; NVKR owns their build and release evidence.

The preview needs explicit operator configuration: API authentication is off and the API uses plain HTTP after installation. Configure API authentication and protected access before admitting callers. The management cluster does not upgrade, scale or replace itself, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup/restore procedure. FDE node images are for evaluation and provide no data-at-rest confidentiality. Read the known limitations before choosing an evaluation or installation path.

The diagram shows the NVKE product family, how it sits on NICo and your GPU machines, and which components talk to each other.

NVKE is not a Kubernetes distribution and not a Cluster API flavour. It is a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters: a throwaway seed cluster stands up a management cluster, and the management plane on it then provisions and lifecycle-manages many isolated workload clusters on demand.

An installation has two kinds of Kubernetes cluster:

  • The runs the NVKE management plane and infrastructure controllers. forms it using a temporary seed cluster; installing the management-plane services is a separate step.
  • run customer applications. The management plane creates and operates them through NICo, Cluster API and the node agent.

Use , the version pinned in go.work, and . Public Go modules must be reachable on the first build. Flox is optional and supplies the repository's development tools; on macOS, it also supplies GNU Make 4. See Development for toolchain setup.

git clone https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvke.git
cd nvke
make build

This builds the workspace and writes nine binaries to : , , , , , , , and . Building does not start a management plane or create a cluster. The node agent runs on Linux.

Contributions, bug reports and documentation improvements are welcome. Start with CONTRIBUTING.md; open an issue before substantial work so maintainers can agree on the approach.

items.content:
A context-compression plugin for month-long single sessions (billions of tokens) ,small context windows (a 100K context is enough) and token savings (5x fewer tokens) .上下文压缩插件，月级长会话会话， 兼顾小窗口(100k上下文足矣)省token(省5倍token) . billion-context is all you need

Context-compression plugin — billion-context is all you need.

small context windows (100K is enough) · · month-long single sessions (billions of tokens) · high compression quality

npm install -g billion-context --prefix=~/.local

Cache health at a glance: a healthy session keeps a prefix-cache hit rate — compression itself costs ≤2%. Sustained lower? Check attribution with or (see FAQ); usual causes, in order: upstream cache TTL expiry · model switch · a bili bug (please report) · other/unknown.

QQ Group: 1056132097 (full) 1108730198 (full) 1129868472 (open)

📝 The paper itself is open-sourced under the MIT License as part of the codebase (). It is a living document — anyone may edit it; improvements are welcome via pull request.

A production-scale longitudinal study: 4.5 months, three hosts, 174,327 model calls, 18.76B cumulative input tokens (~24.7B across all hosts), zero window violations on 204,800-token models, marathon sessions of 8,584–12,049 calls.

📊 Independent Third-Party Benchmarks

  • (中文版) — head-to-head comparison of () against context and 3 RAG arms (, , ) with , , , and : ( Utilized F1, cost vs ), +16.6% over best RAG on LongMemEval-S ( vs , independent-session cost vs ), and 100% survival on 1.48M-token MemoryAgentBench TTL ( steady-state compression where fails ).

sits between agent and its model API, rewriting Anthropic/OpenAI streams with acp-kernel compression. The model decides and to compress into high-fidelity summaries — not a hard truncation limit.

Long coding sessions blow up context. Each provider charges per token, and once you pass the context window the session degrades or dies. compresses consumed conversation into layered summaries so you can run a single session for days — billions of tokens through one context window.

Unlike a host's built-in summarizer, compression here is incremental, reversible, and prefix-cache friendly: summaries are written in small ranges, can be decompressed on demand, and the cache prefix stays intact.

The proxy injects four context-management tools into the conversation; the model calls them itself as context grows, and the proxy executes server-side so folded ranges stay summarized in history until restored:

  • — fold a message range into a detailed summary.
  • — restore a compressed range when exact details are needed again.
  • — keyword search over compressed summaries and visible messages.
  • — context-usage overview plus which ranges are still compressible.
via (built-in plugin) or (self-spawning native plugin, no launcher)

(launcher — the full zero-config posture) or bili plugin install codex (MCP-shell tools companion: — the shell never spawns a proxy and never routes codex's own traffic) — details: docs/clients.md

via (cert-MITM) or prefix — no native mode (event hooks only, no model-request seam, #1050)
via (cert-MITM) or prefix — no native mode (shell-command-only hooks, no tool-injection seam, #1048)
(GitHub Copilot CLI) (launcher, cert-MITM) — closed Go binary, no plugin seam (#1049)
(launcher, cert-MITM) — closed Go binary, no plugin seam (#1049)
(launcher, cert-MITM) — Rust shell + Node agent server, no plugin seam; model traffic is the Responses wire on runtime.<region>.kiro.dev, gateway quirks handled built-in — details: docs/clients.md
(launcher, cert-MITM) — open-source Go binary, no plugin seam; built-in provider hosts whitelisted, custom s auto-discovered from crush.json (#2340)
(launcher, cert-MITM) — open-source Rust editor, no plugin seam; reqwest honors HTTPS_PROXY, CA via SSL_CERT_FILE (Linux env probing); built-in provider hosts whitelisted, custom s auto-discovered from settings.json; loopback providers (ollama/lmstudio) stay direct via NO_PROXY (#2340)

(no context hook)

Native mode vs standalone extensions. The host-native plugins () and the standalone in-process extensions (, ) are — both active means double compression. The installer makes the switch: it replaces the legacy entries (bare name, alias, versioned, path form; array or object shape) and snapshots the original config to once; a install is not touched — remove that one by hand. As a runtime safety net for manual installs, the native entries set BILLION_CONTEXT_NATIVE=<host> synchronously at load so a standalone extension can stand down at action time. On the pi side the marker needs , and the pi-native entry scans both pi settings files once its proxy is up and warns loudly when it spots a co-resident legacy entry the installer never saw — that warning is the only visible signal while an old silently double-compresses.

Linux / macOS — install with a user-level prefix (no , no npm config changes, and 's self-update never hits permission errors):

npm install -g billion-context --prefix=~/.local

The command lands in — already on PATH in most distros; if not, add export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" to or . On nvm or Homebrew Node the default prefix is already user-owned — a plain npm install -g billion-context works as-is. On Windows the default prefix () is also user-writable — plain npm install -g billion-context.

This installs the command ( is kept as an alias). Hitting with an old root-owned prefix? Reinstall with (pass the flag again on any future npm reinstall of ) — that is the permanent fix; avoid .

Prefer containers? A ships at the repository root — see Running in Docker below.

Three ways to use it — pick one:

  • Native plugin (most native):bili plugin install <client> — bili becomes a plugin inside the client; start the client as usual.
  • one command brings up the proxy and the client together — no real config file is ever touched.
  • URL change (most universal): prefix your client's baseURL with the proxy origin + .

Mechanism details behind these three options (plugin lifecycle, runtime-info protocol, injection priority) live in docs/technical-notes.md.

Ports, briefly (#1660): (manual) owns . Everything a lane spawns for you (native hooks, launcher lanes) lives in a separate self-managed zone starting at — collisions hop +1 and each lane remembers its drift, so zero-config installs never fight you for a port, and a deliberate daemon is attached by default. Attach is lane-aware (#2905): a hook rides its own lane's instance first, NEVER another declared lane's — except lanes you list in native.attachLanePriority — and the 8787 user-zone daemon stays the LAST-resort fallback. An upgrade-restart that finds the previous build still draining on the lane's port waits for it to release (up to 5s) and rebinds the SAME port instead of drifting (#1723); only a genuinely occupied port hops +1 — and that hop is now logged loudly.

Option 1 — Native plugin ( / / / / / / )

The proxy lives inside the client: install once, then start the client exactly as you always do — no launcher command, no env vars, no fixed port, no URL edits. Supported today for , , (1.x and 2.x), , , and :

bili plugin install pi          # registers a "billion-context" entry in pi's settings (npm form when bili itself was npm-installed)
bili plugin install omp         # registers an extensions entry in omp's config.yml (~/.omp/agent/config.yml)
bili plugin install opencode    # registers the plugin in opencode's real config + disables native auto-compaction
bili plugin install dsh         # runs 'dsh plugin --profile <name> add billion-context' for every existing profile
bili plugin install kimi        # writes $KIMI_CODE_HOME/plugins/managed/billion-context/kimi.plugin.json (+ installed.json record); per-session routing block lands in config.toml on first start (Kimi Code >= 2.0.0)
bili plugin install hermes      # copies the Python plugin into ~/.hermes/plugins/billion-context/ (+ machine-owned bili.json sidecar) and enables it via `hermes plugins enable billion-context`
bili plugin install zcode       # writes hooks.enabled + a SessionStart hook + mcp.servers.bili into ~/.zcode/cli/config.json; per-session routing lands in the bigmodel provider store on first start
bili plugin remove <client>     # undo (dsh removes through the same channel; config snapshots go to .bili-bak)

Where a client has its own plugin channel you can also install natively, skipping bili commands entirely:

  • dsh plugin --profile <name> add billion-context is the very command drives per profile (npm form only; a git checkout has no published entry — pasting a GitHub address installs source without and the bundle never loads) — same end state either way (pnpm into the profile, bundled patch layer mounted by dsh itself); remove through the same channel. See the dsh section below.

  • easiest is bili plugin install opencode (it picks the right entry form for your host version). Hand-install without bili (npm form only; a git checkout has no published entry):

    • — add the bare npm name to your real config's plugin list: "plugin": ["billion-context"]. The package publishes → dist/agent/opencode-native.js, so opencode loads it through its own Npm.add machinery and the plugin self-spawns exactly like the bili-installed form.

    • — the bare name does NOT work: 2.x resolves it through the package field (, the CLI — no plugin definition), so the module load fails (#3976). Instead, put a one-line re-export in a directory and point the config's list at that directory:

      // <shim dir>/index.js
export { default } from "<abs path to the global install>/dist/agent/opencode-native.js";

      { "plugins": ["<shim dir>"] }

    Either generation: do the two things the bili installer would have done for you too — set "compaction": { "auto": false } in the same config (otherwise OpenCode's native auto-compaction double-compresses) and keep a manual backup of the file first.

  • this repository doubles as a Claude Code plugin marketplace — /plugin marketplace add ranxianglei/billion-context, then /plugin install billion-context@billion-context, then run /billion-context:bili-setup (it drives bili plugin install claude for you and tells you to restart). Same end state as the bili installer; the plugin ships no hooks or MCP entries of its own, so nothing double-registers.

For pi / omp / kimi / claude there is no client-side channel — bili plugin install <client> writes their config entries for you (kimi's declarative + registry record, claude's managed settings block, …).

  • Native mode is with the standalone in-process extensions (, ) — the installer swaps the entries and snapshots the original config ().
  • native installs wire in built-in subagents by default ( / / ) — how to disable them while keeping context compression: Pi built-in subagents.
  • OpenCode legacy sessions, V1/V2 shapes and caveats: OpenCode.
  • reports runtime-info at bootstrap only (static headers can't carry per-request window/model values); subagent tool calls are routed by the proxy's outbound tool-use witness ring (#1685) — no model-visible conversation id.
  • 's native plugin is Python: it points hermes' httpx stack at the proxy via env vars after a health check and stamps per-request headers through an middleware.
  • is the one client a plugin install cannot make self-sufficient: codex routes model traffic via env only (no config-file routing seam for the default ChatGPT-login provider — a managed block would force API-key auth and drop subscription login), and an MCP server cannot inject env into its parent. bili plugin install codex writes a single block into (command = node, args = dist/mcp.js) exposing the four ACP tools; at session start the shell resolves a proxy — env > the live-instance record (any lane's proxy or a daemon) > the 8787 user-zone default (#1660 removed the install-time origin bake, #403) — nothing reachable → fails with -32003. So: start bili first ( or any client's lane proxy), export HTTPS_PROXY yourself if you also want compression, or use for the zero-config full posture. Mechanics: docs/clients.md.
  • has a native posture (#964): managed settings block + hook + MCP shell; the hook rides the self-managed port zone (#1660) and re-pins the managed URL to the live origin each session, so port drift self-heals. Since #1821 the MCP shell also watches the proxy mid-session (30 s tick × 3 failures) and respawns a dead lane proxy itself, so model requests recover within ~90 s instead of a new session (same semantics as the zcode lane). Opt out with (passthrough). Mechanics: docs/technical-notes.md. Known limitation (#2290): the Claude Desktop app's Code tab (CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=claude-desktop) sets its own on its embedded Claude Code, overriding the managed one — desktop sessions bypass the proxy entirely while the managed block's still applies, so they get neither bili compression nor native auto-compaction. The hook warns loudly at session start (and records it for , which also flags machines where Claude Desktop is installed alongside the native lane); terminal sessions are unaffected. Field-tested 2026-10-06 (#2290): putting in the settings block produced zero CONNECT traffic to a live MITM-enabled proxy on Claude Desktop 2.19675.1 / embedded CC 2.1.288 (Windows 11) — the variable reaches no network stack there, matching the CLI behavior of that era — note that newer builds (CC 2.1.301+) DO honour on the CLI, which is why routes via the base-URL rewrite — the launcher gives this lane no proxy and no CA at all, and a child that brings a proxy of its own gets the loopback hosts merged into / so that leg stays direct regardless of its proxy behavior (#3446). As of that version there is no usable routing seam on the desktop Code tab; the lane stays tracked in #2290 in case upstream changes behavior. Account-bound features (#4693): because the lane routes via a custom , Claude Code treats the session as third-party/API-key and disables features bound to your Anthropic account/Cloud — (, driving a local session from mobile/desktop/web) disappears from the command list while bili routes traffic. Compression is unaffected; run plain without bili (or bili plugin remove claude) for sessions that need those features. This is inherent to the base-URL routing seam — no alternative interception point survives CC's undici stack (#2290) — not a config deletion. Desktop-only users can restore native auto-compact with bili plugin remove claude. Since #5095 the managed block also installs a hook (node <root>/dist/claude-subagent-hook.js) that mints a per-dispatch lane token into each subagent's context: subagents that ride the parent's session id with no agent-id headers (the VS Code extension build, #4352) key onto their own compression lanes, so parallel same-type dispatches stop merging (and the token disappears from later requests once the first message folds — those fall back to the fingerprint lane). Uninstall removes the hook with the managed block.
  • has a native posture (#1145): managed block + per-session provider rewrite. Full mechanics: docs/clients.md.
  • and have no native mode (no plugin/MCP/tool-injection seam: #962, #1048) — use / .
  • , and are launcher-only (#1049); goose cannot be cert-MITMed (rustls trusts no CA file) and rides plain-HTTP base-URL redirects instead.

Option 2 — Launcher ( / / / / / / / / / / / / / / / / / / / / / )

The launcher wraps a client in one command: it starts a proxy on an independent port (a fresh instance is always spawned — a port is never reused), then points the client at it — where the client honors proxy/CA env vars, or an isolated where it doesn't. No real config file is ever edited; the client's own config is READ to discover which HTTPS upstream hosts it talks to, and those hosts are whitelisted for MITM so the proxy can TLS-terminate exactly them and blind-tunnel everything else.

bili pi                               # launch pi through the proxy — file-free (#535): env + extension registerProvider, real ~/.pi untouched
bili codex                            # launch codex through the proxy
bili claude                           # launch claude through the proxy
bili omp                              # pi-style, file-free (#535): env + extension registerProvider + compaction cancel, real ~/.omp untouched
bili opencode                         # OpenCode (1.x & 2.x): full guide in the [OpenCode](docs/clients.md#opencode) section below
bili hermes                           # file-free (#535): hermes proxy env (HTTPS_PROXY + combined CA bundle via SSL_CERT_FILE) — https via CONNECT MITM, http via absolute-form forward proxy; real ~/.hermes untouched
bili dsh                              # deepseek-harness: full native plugin injected via --patch (#941) — real dsh tools, session-bound /acp + /acp-cache (plugin mode); non-loopback upstreams ride proxy envs, loopback keeps the overlay DSH_HOME rewrite (#535); dsh auto-compaction off everywhere — host plane via the bundle patch, web-profile presets at load time (#1772/#2474/#3354)
bili codebuddy                        # Tencent CodeBuddy Code CLI: CODEBUDDY_BASE_URL /bili/ rewrite (OpenAI chat completions wire), budget aligned via CODEBUDDY_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW; real ~/.codebuddy untouched
bili qoder                            # qoder CLI (`qoder`/`qodercli`): model endpoint is hardcoded https (no /bili/ rewrite possible) — cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, default model hosts whitelisted (#653). Qoder Desktop is a separate BYOK/custom channel that speaks plaintext OpenAI over a `/bili/` prefix — point it at bili as a normal custom provider (not this MITM lane); its official-subscription traffic is encrypted and out of scope (#764)
bili trae                             # Trae CLI (ByteDance, closed Go binary, no base-URL override) — cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE, model host from TRAE_CLI_API_HOST or the default enterprise gateway (#655)
bili jcode                            # jcode (Rust agent harness) — env-only cert-MITM launch: HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE, model host api.z.ai whitelisted, local loopback providers stay direct via NO_PROXY
bili kimi                             # Kimi Code CLI (Moonshot): standard proxy envs except an unconditional loopback bypass — https via cert-MITM, http via absolute-form forward proxy; loopback endpoints inventoried with a manual /bili/ hint (#757)
bili gemini                           # Gemini CLI (Google): GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL /bili/ rewrite to generativelanguage.googleapis.com (Google native wire), real ~/.gemini untouched
bili iflow                            # iFlow CLI: IFLOW_BASE_URL /bili/ rewrite to apis.iflow.cn/v1 (OpenAI chat-completions wire), real ~/.iflow untouched
bili qwen                             # Qwen Code (multi-protocol gemini-cli fork, no base-URL hook): cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, default DashScope/Qwen model hosts whitelisted, custom relays via --mitm-domain
bili antigravity                      # Antigravity CLI (agy, Google): CLOUD_CODE_URL /bili/ rewrite of daily-cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com — the real default upstream (bare cloudcode-pa 400s on /v1internal:*, #3129); undocumented language-server env override, v2.19.1 binary-verified; wire recognized as Google native by path (#2115)
bili mcode                            # MiniMax Code CLI: same shape as kimi (proxy envs, unconditional loopback bypass, cert-MITM/absolute-form); session bound via X-Mavis-Session-Id (#1050)
bili aider                            # Aider (Python pair programmer): cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE/REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE; endpoint from OPENAI_API_BASE / ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL / --openai-api-base / .aider.conf.yml (#1048)
bili copilot                          # Copilot CLI (GitHub, closed Go binary) — cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE, api.githubcopilot.com + per-plan subdomains whitelisted (#1049)
bili amp                              # Amp CLI (Sourcegraph, closed Go binary) — cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE, ampcode.com whitelisted (#1049)
bili goose                            # Goose (Block, Rust/reqwest): rustls release builds trust no CA file — openai/anthropic legs via OPENAI_HOST/ANTHROPIC_HOST, custom providers via a regenerated GOOSE_PATH_ROOT overlay (/bili/ rewrites, real config untouched) (#1049)
bili kiro                             # Kiro CLI (AWS): cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + combined CA on SSL_CERT_FILE and NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS; only runtime.<region>.kiro.dev is decrypted; developer/system items re-voiced as user for the gateway; session = Kiro's conversation id (survives --resume)
bili pi --mitm-domain api.foo.com     # add a domain to the MITM whitelist

Option 3 — URL change ( prefix)

Then just prefix your client's existing baseURL with http://localhost:8787/bili/. The full upstream URL is embedded in the path, so the proxy knows where to forward without any config:

client baseURL before:  https://api.openai.com/v1
client baseURL after:   http://localhost:8787/bili/https://api.openai.com/v1

With the proxy running and your config saved, check it answers and that your first real request shows compression activity in the log:

# Health check (proxy up + where it forwards)
curl -s http://localhost:8787/__bili/health
# → {"ok":true,"upstream":"https://api.anthropic.com"}

# Live session stats (after a real request)
curl -s http://localhost:8787/__bili/stats

Then send one message from your client and watch the log (~/.local/state/billion-context/bili.log, also printed to stderr). You should see a line per request, and once the conversation grows, [acp-usage] round N input=X cached=Y (cache hit Z%) + a event.

Everything that doesn't fit in one Quickstart line — how each client's lanes attach, what gets written where, and known limitations — lives in : dsh · Kimi Code · Hermes · ZCode · Gemini family (Gemini CLI / iFlow CLI / Qwen Code / Antigravity) · cert-MITM clients that never compress (CONNECT blind tunnels, #897) · unrecognized endpoints going direct (#1290) · OpenCode (launcher / native / pure proxy, status & rules, legacy opencode-acp sessions #920).

From source (development)

is the development branch and can be broken at any moment — unreleased changes, failing builds, unverified fixes. Unless you are patching the code or testing an unreleased fix, install a release with npm as above.

git clone https://github.com/ranxianglei/billion-context.git
cd billion-context
npm ci
npm run build
npm link
bili --version

After , works from any directory.

How do I check my cache hit rate? Don't dig through logs — prints a text summary report right in the client, headed by a clickable : open it for the web version of the session page — the cache hit-rate plus per-break :

The report has four blocks that pin things down at a glance: (totals + hit% with an explicit verdict; misses decomposed into new content / compress re-pay / upstream-ttl-or-client-rewrite) · (per-fold economics: net tokens saved, paid-back verdicts) · (anomalies only: hit<85% or miss≥5000). Rule of thumb: compression itself costs ≤2% — a healthy session sits at . When you see less, the attribution tells you which of the usual suspects it was, in this order: ① upstream cache TTL expiry (shows up as stable-prefix misses — the top-spikes line names idle times), ② a model switch, ③ a bili bug (report it with the page attached), ④ other/unknown. lists every fold & line; same report over Since #1535 the report ends with a section: a mid-session model change invalidates the provider's prefix cache, so the whole stable prefix is re-billed on the next request — each switch's unexplained residual (its bucket minus new content) is charged to the switch instead of masquerading as TTL expiry; per-event , hit %, and attributed tokens are listed ( lists every event, the summary the last 8), and the web sessions table gains a matching model-switch column. Since #2131 the same machinery fingerprints the outbound credential (a 12-hex sha256 of the /-family headers — the raw key is never stored) and attributes a — the relay behind a stable URL rotated to a different account — in a dedicated section, a line in , and a 🔑 badge in the web sessions column. HTTP: ; the raw per-request lines still land in the log file for deep dives.

In clients with the native plugin (opencode, dsh, hermes), renders the ACP status panel of the current conversation straight from the proxy (session, blocks, compressible ranges, usage); before the first model request it shows an idle notice instead. prints the cache report above.

Can I query sessions and config over the web? Yes — open http://localhost:8787: an overview dashboard, session list with per-session detail, live logs, a config editor, and an upstream connectivity test. A Blog view renders notes and long-form articles inside the panel itself — bundled with the install, refreshed from GitHub master on a ~1-hour throttle while online (fail-soft to the bundled copy when offline); the full library also lives on GitHub Pages. Everything else is also plain JSON for scripting (, , , …).

When does compression happen? It is model-driven: the injected context tools are called by the model as context grows, gentle growth nudges (~50K-token steps by design, adjustable via compress.nudgeGrowthTokens) prompt it along the way, and preflight fires as a hard backstop when the input alone exceeds the window (#470). Watch it live with or the web UI.

Does compression shrink my client's own conversation file? No — the most common surprise in very long sessions (#5796). Compression shrinks what is sent to the model: every outgoing request is rebuilt from live blocks plus summaries, so the wire stays small however long the conversation runs. The client's stored history is user data — bili never rewrites it. On dsh the host's auto-compaction is additionally disabled while bili is active (two compressors must not fight over one history, #1772/#2474/#3354), so the host-side file grows with every turn: each turn takes longer as it grows (measured: tens of seconds per turn at ~30K messages, #5796), and the practical convergence path is to when it gets heavy. The web session list badges sessions at 5,000+ requests (长会话/slow) as a reminder that this point has been reached.

Why does the first compaction wait until ~200k? Compaction does not trigger on absolute window position but on growth intervals: by default the first soft compaction fires 50k tokens past the boot content (compress.nudgeGrowthTokens, flat and window-independent). With a boot around 100k — or with the growth step set to ~100k — the first compaction may wait until ~200k. To make it fire earlier: 1) trim the system prompt, disable unneeded tools, prune skills; 2) lower compress.nudgeGrowthTokens to ~50k; 3) enable lean mode. Worked example in docs/configuration.md.

Is bili transparent? How do I turn it off? Unrecognized endpoints forward unchanged (docs/clients.md), and every mode reverses cleanly: bili plugin remove <client> for native installs, stop using the launcher command / env vars / prefix for the other two — traffic goes direct again immediately.

Can I combine bili with a model-routing gateway (e.g. magpie)? Yes — point the client at bili, and point bili at the gateway through the prefix, which embeds the gateway's absolute URL: http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425…. Example: Claude Code → ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425 + ; OpenAI-style clients → OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1 (+ ). Compression happens routing — every request that reaches any account in the gateway's routing groups is already compressed. Credentials stay in the gateway: the client's dummy key rides through untouched, and real keys never touch bili. Connection lifecycle tuning (#1982)

Client-facing connections close gracefully after the final response: when the proxy initiates the close (), it waits up to BILI_POST_RESPONSE_LINGER_MS (default ) for the client's close signal before releasing the socket, so pooled clients see a clean EOF instead of a possible RST from racing bytes. Related knobs: BILI_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT_MS (idle-reap budget, default ) and BILI_CLIENT_ERROR_BACKSTOP_MS (terminal backstop for the error-drain path, default ) — full semantics in docs/configuration.md.

The proxy checks npm on startup and every 3 minutes; a newer version is installed in place and a notice is logged — , unless you enable opt-in self-restart ( flag, env ACP_AUTO_RESTART_ON_UPDATE=1, or "autoRestartOnUpdate": true in config — default OFF): with zero in-flight requests it verifies the new install, stops accepting connections, drains, spawns a replacement on the same port, and exits once it accepts connections (clients reconnect automatically; session state survives on disk). Safety gates: zero in-flight through the drain window, an install sanity check before re-exec, and a 10-minute cooldown marker so a flapping version can never loop-restart; any failure resumes the original listener and falls back to the plain reminder.

Staggered rollout (#3619): a discovered version is not applied immediately by automatic updates. Each instance draws ONE random moment inside a delay window (built-in default ) and upgrades when it arrives; the drawn moment is persisted, so restarts never re-roll. Fleet upgrades therefore spread across the window instead of completing within minutes of a release, leaving time to catch a bad release mid-rollout (#3401/#3600/#3394). The window plus emergency controls live in a public policy file ( in this repo, fetched anonymously with ETag caching): freezes automatic upgrades fleet-wide, skips listed versions, sets an upgrade ceiling. Fail-open by design — an unreachable or malformed file simply falls back to local defaults, and the file can steer timing/skip/pin only, never what gets installed. Per-machine exits: manual bypasses /stagger (still respects /), + (or BILI_UPDATE_STAGGER_MIN_MS/BILI_UPDATE_STAGGER_MAX_MS) restore legacy immediate upgrades, and disables auto-updates entirely. Full format and semantics: docs/configuration.md → .

In ( / / — the proxy runs embedded in a long-lived host), "restart bili" means restarting the : the embedded process cannot exit on its own, so a host left open keeps serving whatever code it started with, silently missing every fix auto-update reports as installed (#1603). Auto-update only ever replaces disk files and (optionally) the proxy process; injected code inside the host process only takes effect after the host itself restarts — so if the injection breaks at runtime mid-session (a disposed agent scope, a disabled plugin), model traffic goes direct and uncompressed until then. Since #3581 this state is visible instead of silent: the web UI shows a "takeover broken" banner (agent + refusal count) whenever a plugin reports its attribution gate degraded while no session is live, and / expose the per-agent state (//, refusal count, first-refusal timestamp). Background lanes that are agentless (e.g. dsh's title-generation sidecar) never carry an initiator, so their small one-shot calls go direct by definition; under the #3651 contract these normal interceptions are NEVER reported and therefore can never raise the banner. The banner fires only when the attribution lookup itself throws (an internal host error, e.g. a disposed agent scope), and then names what failed: the thrown error text, the masked endpoint, when the episode started, how many requests went uncompressed, the remedy (restart the host process), plus copy/submit-diagnostics buttons that prefill a GitHub issue.

Update visibility is silent by default since v0.1.183 (#1977): routine/recommended releases no longer render an update line on the panel footer or in — only a -tier release surfaces there (CRITICAL UPDATE READY/AVAILABLE). The standing ways to check an installed-but-not-restarted release are the stale cues above: web UI banner, the one-line warning, and . Deliberately no always-on nag; the advisory channel (#1481) remains the only auto-visible critical path.

When an install keeps failing (unwritable or host-managed dir, network error, …), auto-update no longer re-downloads and retries on every 3-minute cycle forever. After three consecutive failures it backs off exponentially (5 min → 10 → 20 …, capped at 6 h), logs a one-time actionable hint (fix permissions / npm prefix, reinstall user-level, or disable via / ), and logs nothing further about the failure while cooling down (no download, no retry line); it resumes as soon as the failure clears or a different version is targeted (#1603).

The same bounded retry now covers the the global self-update drives instead of writing the copy itself — the dsh desktop in-place copy, the dsh profile bundles, and pi's npm copy (#2192). Each lane keeps its own failure streak keyed by lane + target version, so a persistently broken desktop layout no longer re-downloads the full tarball every cycle (up to ~480 downloads/day per affected machine before the fix); three strikes arms the same exponential cooldown, and the one-time hint names the failing lane and its manual fix (dsh plugin --profile <name> add …, , or recreate the desktop profile). Host-managed instances additionally check on their own slower cadence — 30 minutes plus up to 15 minutes of jitter, tracked under a separate throttle marker — instead of consuming the global 3-minute budget. Failure streaks are shared across every bili process on the machine through a small state file in the cache dir (), so several running instances don't each burn their own retry budget; a clean disarms the dsh profile lane immediately. The file is written atomically (tmp+rename) and every writer merges with what is already on disk, so concurrent instances cooperate instead of overwriting each other's streaks; long-lived processes re-read it when it changes, so a manual disarm by one copy is visible to the others on their next check. It is fail-safe in the retry direction — a corrupt file or jumped clock is dropped, never allowed to silence a lane for long. clears the dsh-profile lane's key; a repaired desktop lane clears its own key on its next successful in-place refresh.

Stale local DNS after a network/VPN change (#5224)

A standalone proxy can keep holding stale OS-resolver state after a WSL/VPN/TUN topology change — the process caches its system resolver and libuv's does not re-read on its own. Symptom: every model request through the tunnel answers HTTP 502 tunnel_destination_denied with detail , even though a freshly started resolves the same host fine at that moment and from a new shell works. Either remedy clears it:

  • Restart the proxy process — a fresh process re-reads the system resolver. In the launcher lanes and the dsh web-profile lane the proxy is a process (the instance registry), so restarting only the client/host re-adopts the same wedged proxy and does help — you must stop and relaunch the proxy itself. (In embedded plugin mode the proxy runs inside the host, so restarting the host clear it.)
  • Route egress through an upstream proxy — or BILI_UPSTREAM_PROXY=… BILI_UPSTREAM_PROXY_MODE=auto: the destination is then resolved remotely by that proxy, so bili never consults its own (stale) resolver for admission.

Header-less clients (pi-like): anonymous prefix affinity. With no conversation signal at all, the proxy resolves the session from the replayed history itself (, #309): a request reattaches to a stored session only when its history reproduces that session's message chain byte-exactly from position 0; otherwise it gets its own deterministic session. Consequences (#1262): a conversation reattaches to its own session (even after a proxy restart, #499); a new task with an identical opener does NOT inherit another conversation's blocks — it mints a fresh, fully separate session; a request with no usable signal at all gets an explicit 400 instead of silently colliding.

For upstream sticky-routing, the proxy forwards only identity values the client already supplied (e.g. a body is forwarded upstream as ); it never synthesizes one itself.

explicit-id clients are safe to run concurrently. For header-less multi-agent use, prefer the client plugin (stamps a stable id per conversation) or pass an explicit header — otherwise prefix affinity still keeps distinct tasks apart (a diverged fork costs one raw resend plus a compression-ladder restart).

Derived (child) sessions inherit the parent's compressed context (#1333, #1362)

A child session (subagent/fork starting from an empty history) reports its lineage at birth — its identity registration carries and the proxy records a read-only link — so / fall back along the parent chain for content the child never saw itself (cycle-guarded, depth cap 8). Nothing is copied into the child, the parent is never modified; if the parent is unknown the child simply starts fresh. Per-lane parent signals (pi/omp header, OpenCode V1/V2 ): docs/session-identity.md. claude/codex/dsh need nothing here: they share one session id across subagents or have no child-session concept at all.

Running multiple instances (#3633)

One conversation belongs to one instance for its whole life. Fold state, prefix affinity and the summary budget are keyed to a session id whose home is the client's own history — and the session's rows live in that instance's . There is no shared store between instances: nothing replicates, nothing fails over, nothing rehydrates a session onto a different instance.

Consequences for anyone tempted to put several instances behind one Service:

  • Sticky routing is required, and affinity is the wrong kind. The conversation identity lives in a header or the request body, not the source IP — a Service can only hash on IP, so a client pinned to replica N silently loses session when replica N dies (buying throughput while selling away availability, exactly when you scaled out because of load). Correct routing is an L7 proxy hashing a conversation header (x-bili-plugin-conversation, , , …) onto a backend — and the client actually sending one (header-less clients get prefix affinity instead, which an L7 proxy cannot hash).
  • Instance count is volume count. The state directory is one local directory with SQLite in WAL mode (); a coherent shared and working byte-range locks across writers require an RWO volume that is never shared. Pointing two instances at the same RWX/NFS path does not give you a shared store — it gives you silent corruption behind a timeout. One RWO volume per instance, included: "unified" means one store (sessions + CCR + CAS in one ), not one store for the fleet.
  • The workload that actually scales is many independent short-lived conversations — one proxy per client or per lane — not one long conversation load-balanced across proxies. Long conversations are single-instance by design.

Single machine, multiple installs (#5046). The topology above covers deployment replicas; one desktop has a sibling situation: two installs on ONE machine (e.g. two DSH profiles — desktop + bot, or a global npm copy beside a host-tree copy) each start their own proxy and, unless isolated, both resolve the SAME default XDG sessions directory and the same config file. Multiple processes writing ONE local-disk is the SUPPORTED topology (#5082/#5091) — SQLite WAL is multi-process safe on a local filesystem — so startup NEVER blocks on a live foreign writer: the peer shows up as an info-level [storage] process pid … is also using … line plus the status wire, nothing more (policy settled 2026-10-31, withdrawing the #5046/B-era refuse-to-start for exactly this shape). What genuinely remains hazardous is two installs walking the SAME concurrently — that case alarms separately (split-brain contest, #3923). If you still want strictly separate histories and stores per install, give each its own (plus when the config should differ too) through that install's launcher/profile environment — no global env changes needed. Once isolated, the notice drops off entirely. Note the distinction from the deployment case above: local disk with SQLite WAL tolerates many writers; shared RWX/NFS storage does NOT and keeps requiring one writer per volume.

The proxy rewrites each session's state file every turn of a long session; on Windows, real-time AV (Defender), the search indexer, or a sync tool (OneDrive) can lock the sessions dir mid-write, so persists fail with until the lock clears. The same exclusion also covers the unified-storage refusing to open (unable to open database file, #3823) — the storage-degrade warning names it as the first suspect.

Session file cleanup (#1082)

Short-lived sessions leave small state files behind that are never resumed. Cleanup is (; off by default — session files are user data, no silent deletion policy): when enabled, bili sweeps the sessions dir at boot and hourly and deletes a file only when BOTH hold — older than BILI_SESSION_GC_MAX_AGE_DAYS (default 7 days) AND never compressed with its newest request body ≤ BILI_SESSION_GC_MAX_TOKENS tokens (default 1M) — so deletion loses nothing but bytes. CCR content stores follow their session file's lifecycle; compressed sessions are never deleted; every deletion is audit-logged. Full policy: docs/configuration.md.

Storage maintenance CLI (#3928)

The same store maintenance the panel exposes over HTTP (, POST /__bili/storage/restore) has a thin CLI layer — no proxy needed, run it on any machine that owns the sessions dir:

bili sessions ls                 # id, label, decoded size, last-updated, storage status (active/archived)
bili sessions rm <id>            # full delete (content refcount release incl. media); shrinks index.db afterwards (--no-vacuum skips)
bili sessions archive <id>       # export to archive/archive.jsonl + sweep rows; tombstone keeps label & identity
bili sessions restore <id>       # bring an archived session back from the log line
bili sessions foreign-blocks     # (#5312) list fold blocks whose covered messages never belonged to this transcript — dry-run; --apply reversibly archives them, --restore <sid>:<bid> brings one back
bili storage gc [--days N] [--vacuum full|incremental] [--dry-run]
                                 # print the sweep plan (sessions past retention, zero-ref content rows, ~pages reclaimable), then run the same gc() the HTTP endpoint calls; --dry-run stops after the plan

// require the unified store (BILI_STORAGE_UNIFIED=shadow|full or in the config file) — legacy-only installs refuse with a hint. defaults to (365). No scheduler: these run on demand. All commands accept .

Full vacuum is an offline operation on large databases (#4612). (the default) rewrites the entire index.db under an exclusive write lock — O(db size), minutes to tens of minutes on multi-GB databases, with no intermediate progress (SQLite's VACUUM is atomic; it cannot be split). Running it while a proxy is serving from the same sessions dir starves that proxy's writes until its storage layer degrades, so refuses to start when another live process holds the database ( pid discipline, #4175): the CLI exits 1 with an actionable message, the panel endpoint returns HTTP 409. Stop the other instance first (or wait for it to exit) and retry; for online-safe shrink use , which reclaims freed pages in short transactions without taking the exclusive lock. The zero-ref delete sweep itself is batched with per-batch progress output either way.

Early. Protocol handling and compression work against mock tests (500+ passing). Real-model integration testing is the next milestone. Expect rough edges.

Client-side plugins for pi / omp / opencode ship inside () for the cooperative-proxy path. See the section above for how , the standalone , and relate.

Attribution requirement (one term on top of MIT)

This project is MIT-licensed : any product or service (commercial or open source) whose users can see or interact with it and which uses this software must attribute it — stating that it uses billion-context with a link back to this repository — on its home page, documentation, or About/Credits page. Pure server-side/embedded use satisfies this via shipped documentation. See the at the end of LICENSE.

If you build on this project, we'd love to hear about it: open an issue (no obligation) so we can track where it's used.

items.title: mbillow/localthings
items.content:
Control your Samsung appliances from Home Assistant over your home network, with no cloud account.

Control your Samsung appliances from Home Assistant over your home network, with no cloud account.

LocalThings connects Home Assistant to Samsung washers, dryers, refrigerators, air conditioners, ovens and other appliances that work with the SmartThings app. It talks to each appliance on your local network.

  • Appliances that support push send changes as they happen. LocalThings checks the rest every 30 seconds.
  • It works without the internet. After setup, LocalThings never contacts Samsung's servers.
  • LocalThings sends nothing to Samsung. The appliance itself still keeps its own connection to Samsung, and LocalThings doesn't change that.
  • Setup needs an IP address. For most appliances, you enter the address and LocalThings works out the type and model, then creates matching controls and sensors.
Air conditioner, including multi-unit systems
Refrigerator, kimchi refrigerator, wine cellar
Cooktop, gas, radiant electric and induction; some models read-onlyRobot vacuum, early support
Soundbar, media player, settings and status

What you see depends on what each appliance reports. Typical controls and sensors include power, program or mode selection, start, pause and stop, temperatures and setpoints, time remaining and finish time, door and child-lock state, energy use, filter status and alarms.

Most Samsung appliances from about 2022 onward work, and so do some earlier washers, air conditioners and wall ovens that use an older local interface. See Older appliances on TCP 8888. Setup detects which interface an appliance has, and tells you if it finds none.

If an appliance sets up but LocalThings doesn't recognize it, or a control is missing, Home Assistant shows a notice asking for a diagnostics download. That download is usually all the maintainers need to add support. See Reporting a capability gap.

LocalThings uses the standards the appliances implement:

  • Samsung's connected appliances are OCF devices. LocalThings discovers each appliance's resources through and reads its device type, such as , from . Where an appliance offers both a standard OCF resource and a Samsung extension for the same state, LocalThings uses the standard one.
  • LocalThings sends Constrained Application Protocol requests, defined in RFC 7252, over an encrypted DTLS session with an X.509 client certificate. It uses CoAP Observe, RFC 7641, for push updates, and block-wise transfer, RFC 7959, for large responses. The library implements the protocol layer.
  • Home Assistant's own patterns. Setup, reconfigure and reauthentication run in the UI config flow. A data-update coordinator combines push and polling. DHCP discovery follows an appliance to a new IP address. Repairs notices report gaps. LocalThings redacts diagnostics downloads and translates entity names into twelve languages.
  • Declarative appliance maps. Each appliance type is a table that maps the resources an appliance reports to Home Assistant entities. Tests check the tables against 90+ captures from real appliances, so a new model usually needs a table entry and no protocol code.

  1. In HACS, go to , search for , and select . LocalThings is in HACS's default list, so you don't need to add a custom repository.

    Without HACS, copy custom_components/localthings/ into the folder of your Home Assistant config.

  1. Go to Settings > Devices & Services > Add Integration > LocalThings.
  2. Enter the appliance's IP address. For most appliances, that's the whole setup.
  3. LocalThings connects, reads the appliance's type and model, and adds one Home Assistant device for it.

When you add your first appliance, LocalThings contacts Samsung's servers once to read a public identifier. It uses no account or login. Later appliances reuse that identifier, so adding them needs only an IP address and no internet access.

A few appliances need one more step:

  • Some appliances refuse the automatic certificate. Setup then offers to import a pre-shared key, which LocalThings can't obtain for you. Credential acquisition covers where one comes from. We're still working to understand these appliances, and #435 has the plan, what we've found so far, and a place to report how it went. Setup also offers the public CA certificate, which the project's shows how to get, but no appliance that refused the automatic certificate has been reported to accept it.

You can rename devices. LocalThings identifies each appliance by its OCF device ID, not by its name or serial number. Some models ship the same serial number on every unit.

Each appliance has a option in Settings > Devices & Services, with these settings under :

  • "Allow writes even when remote control is reported off". By default, LocalThings refuses a command while the appliance reports remote control off, and shows an error, because the appliance would ignore the command without saying so. Some appliances accept certain commands anyway. Turn this on only after you confirm yours does.
  • "Estimated finish -- minimum change (minutes)". LocalThings holds a washer's, dryer's or dishwasher's finish time until the appliance's estimate changes by at least this many minutes. This keeps one-minute jitter out of your history. The default is 3. Set 0 to report every change.
  • "Remember modes the device reports but doesn't advertise". Some appliances run in a mode they never list as available. With this setting on, which is the default, LocalThings remembers such a mode and keeps offering it. in the same menu clears the list.

An appliance that exposes more than one device, such as each indoor unit of a multi-split system or each cavity of a dual oven, also gets in the same menu. Some appliances report an extra slot that isn't real hardware, which shows up as a duplicate or empty device. Untick it there: LocalThings removes that device and stops reading it. Tick it again to bring it back.

Brief disconnects are normal. Samsung appliances drop their connection for a moment now and then. LocalThings reconnects, and entities keep their last value meanwhile. If reconnects happen several times a minute, check the appliance's Wi-Fi signal. Also check that nothing else on your network holds a connection to it, because an appliance accepts one connection at a time.

Keep appliances registered in SmartThings. If you remove an appliance from SmartThings, it resets its network settings the next time it reaches Samsung's servers. It then drops off Wi-Fi until you set it up in the app again. This happens even if you block its internet access most of the time.

Some washers and dryers stop counting energy without SmartThings. On the DA_WM_TP2_20_COMMON board (for example the WW80T654ALX and DV80T6220LX), the energy total stops increasing while the appliance can't reach SmartThings, and resumes once it reconnects. LocalThings can only show what the appliance records, so if your energy sensor stays at one value while cycles run, check that the appliance can reach Samsung's servers.

Restarting while an appliance is powered off

If Home Assistant restarts while an appliance is off, LocalThings loads the appliance's device and entities from the last successful setup. They show until the appliance answers, then recover without any action from you. This works for any appliance LocalThings has reached at least once. A new appliance must be reachable to set it up.

When an appliance's IP address changes

About half of Samsung's appliances report their Wi-Fi MAC address. For those, Home Assistant's DHCP discovery spots the new address and LocalThings updates the entry. For other appliances, select on the entry and enter the new address. LocalThings checks that the appliance at that address is the right one, and keeps its entities, history and automations. Deleting and re-adding the appliance would lose all three.

Older appliances on TCP 8888

Some appliances from about 2018 to 2022 have a different local interface, HTTPS on TCP port 8888. So far this covers a WW6500 washer, TP6X air conditioners, an NV51K777OS Flex Duo wall oven, an NQ70M6650DS microwave/oven combo, NZ36K7570R and NZ30K7570RS cooktops, and an RF28K9380SR refrigerator. Setup detects the interface from the IP address and then asks for a . Leave the field empty and the appliance issues a token, sending it back to Home Assistant on port 8889. For that to work, switch Remote Control on at the appliance with the door closed, and make sure the appliance can reach Home Assistant on port 8889. If the appliance later rejects its token, Home Assistant asks for a new one.

On the RF28K9380SR refrigerator, when setup asks for the token, hold for about 5 seconds, until "on" shows in the freezer temperature display. It refuses the automatic certificate, so setup then asks for an AC14K_M CA certificate and key, and it needs both to finish.

For the tested NZ36K7570R and NZ30K7570RS cooktops, NV51K777OS oven and NQ70M6650DS combo, if Smart Connect is already on, no token will be returned. Turn it off, request a token in LocalThings, then turn it on.

On these appliances, a chosen cycle, temperature, rinse count or spin speed takes effect only when the cycle starts. The selects hold your choice, and the button sends it. If you turn the dial on the appliance, the dial's setting replaces the held choice.

This interface speaks only TLS 1.0 and presents a certificate LocalThings can't verify, so LocalThings accepts both on this one connection. No other part of LocalThings relaxes TLS.

Starting an oven, range or microwave

An oven only starts when the mode, temperature and cook time arrive together. While it's idle, the mode select, setpoint and cook time hold your choice, starting from the mode's own defaults, and the button sends them. The localthings.start_cooking action does the same in one call, with any value you leave out taken from the mode's defaults. Once a cook is running, changes to the setpoint and cook time go straight to the oven.

Each appliance reports which of its modes a remote may start, and the temperature and time limits for each. LocalThings follows that list, and only offers the modes the oven can run right now. The button appears only on an appliance that reports at least one mode it can start, and a start outside those limits is refused with the allowed range. On a range with two ovens, each oven has its own Start cooking button and starts separately. Some modes can't be started remotely by design: on every microwave seen so far, none of the microwave-power modes can be. Remote Control has to be on at the appliance, and it switches off after a power cut.

Multi-unit air conditioners

Some installations run several indoor units from one outdoor unit, all at one IP address. LocalThings finds the extra units after its first connection. Each unit gets its own Home Assistant device and climate card, linked to the main unit. LocalThings skips the unused slots some systems report. If a unit you expect is missing, attach a diagnostics download to an issue.

Reporting a capability gap

If LocalThings doesn't recognize an appliance, or the appliance reports something LocalThings doesn't handle yet, a notice appears under Settings > System > Repairs. It points you to on the device. LocalThings removes personal and network details from that download before you save it. It removes the account email, tokens, device IDs, MAC addresses, serial numbers, the Wi-Fi network name and password, the device's name, the name of a paired phone and the device's on/off history. You can attach the file to a device-support issue, and that is the fastest way to get an appliance supported.

A diagnostics download can't show whether a command sticks or what order commands need. The localthings.read_resource and localthings.write_resource actions answer those questions by reading and writing an appliance's resources without going through its entities. See Reading and writing resources directly.

We welcome patches, especially:

  • Support for appliance types LocalThings doesn't cover yet, or for models that don't fully work. Start from a diagnostics download. CONTRIBUTING.md covers adding a type.
  • Reports that confirm or rule out more models of a supported type.
  • Protocol-level fixes. These belong upstream in . Fixes to entities, setup, the coordinator or the registry belong here.

Please don't include real device UUIDs, MAC addresses, serial numbers, IP addresses or private keys in a pull request. CONTRIBUTING.md covers the dev environment, the checks to run, the repo layout, and the rules for comments and commits.

items.content:
Hunt down social media accounts by username across social networks

Packages for ParrotOS and Ubuntu 24.04, maintained by a third party, appear to be . Users of these systems should defer to // or Docker.

pipx install sherlock-project or may be used in place of
docker run -it --rm sherlock/sherlock

Community-maintained packages are available for Debian (>= 13), Ubuntu (>= 22.10), Homebrew, Kali, and BlackArch. These packages are not directly supported or maintained by the Sherlock Project.

See all alternative installation methods here.

To search for only one user:

To search for more than one user:

sherlock user1 user2 user3

Accounts found will be stored in an individual text file with the corresponding username (e.g ).

$ sherlock --help
usage: sherlock [-h] [--version] [--verbose] [--folderoutput FOLDEROUTPUT] [--output OUTPUT] [--csv] [--xlsx] [--site SITE_NAME] [--proxy PROXY_URL] [--dump-response]
                [--json JSON_FILE] [--timeout TIMEOUT] [--print-all] [--print-found] [--no-color] [--browse] [--local] [--nsfw] [--txt] [--ignore-exclusions]
                USERNAMES [USERNAMES ...]

Sherlock: Find Usernames Across Social Networks (Version 0.16.0)

positional arguments:
  USERNAMES             One or more usernames to check with social networks. Check similar usernames using {?} (replace to '_', '-', '.').

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --version             Display version information and dependencies.
  --verbose, -v, -d, --debug
                        Display extra debugging information and metrics.
  --folderoutput FOLDEROUTPUT, -fo FOLDEROUTPUT
                        If using multiple usernames, the output of the results will be saved to this folder.
  --output OUTPUT, -o OUTPUT
                        If using single username, the output of the result will be saved to this file.
  --csv                 Create Comma-Separated Values (CSV) File.
  --xlsx                Create the standard file for the modern Microsoft Excel spreadsheet (xlsx).
  --site SITE_NAME      Limit analysis to just the listed sites. Add multiple options to specify more than one site.
  --proxy PROXY_URL, -p PROXY_URL
                        Make requests over a proxy. e.g. socks5://127.0.0.1:1080
  --dump-response       Dump the HTTP response to stdout for targeted debugging.
  --json JSON_FILE, -j JSON_FILE
                        Load data from a JSON file or an online, valid, JSON file. Upstream PR numbers also accepted.
  --timeout TIMEOUT     Time (in seconds) to wait for response to requests (Default: 60)
  --print-all           Output sites where the username was not found.
  --print-found         Output sites where the username was found (also if exported as file).
  --no-color            Don't color terminal output
  --browse, -b          Browse to all results on default browser.
  --local, -l           Force the use of the local data.json file.
  --nsfw                Include checking of NSFW sites from default list.
