items.content:
🚀 PR Agent: The Original Open-Source PR Reviewer. This project is not the Qodo free tier.

The Original Open-Source PR Reviewer

This repository contains the open-source PR Agent Project. It is not the Qodo offering for open-source projects.

PR-Agent is an open-source, AI-powered code review agent and a community-maintained legacy project of Qodo. It is distinct from Qodo's primary AI code review offering, which provides a feature-rich, context-aware experience. Qodo offers a free version for open-source projects and integrates seamlessly with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps for high-quality automated reviews.

PR-Agent is a community-maintained open-source project, with its ongoing development supported by our sponsors. If you'd like to support the project, consider becoming a sponsor.

Docker Hub namespace migration. Releases and later are published under . Older releases (up to and including ) remain available at the legacy namespace as a frozen archive — no new images are pushed there. Update any pinned / / references when upgrading to .

🚀 Quick Start for PR-Agent

1. GitHub Action (Recommended)

Add automated PR reviews to your repository with a simple workflow file:

# .github/workflows/pr-agent.yml
name: PR Agent
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]
jobs:
  pr_agent_job:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - name: PR Agent action step
      uses: the-pr-agent/pr-agent@main
      env:
        OPENAI_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_KEY }}
        GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

2. CLI Usage (Local Development)

Run PR-Agent locally on your repository:

pip install "pr-agent[github]"
export OPENAI_KEY=your_key_here
pr-agent --pr_url https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123 review

Git provider SDKs are optional extras: install the one for your provider (list), or for every integration. Complete CLI setup guide

🎯 Built for Real Development Teams

: Each tool (, , ) uses a single LLM call (~30 seconds, low cost)

: JSON-based prompting allows easy customization of review categories and behavior via configuration files

  • : GitHub, GitLab, BitBucket, Azure DevOps, Gitea
  • : CLI, GitHub Actions, Docker, self-hosted, webhooks
  • : OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Mistral, and any other model reachable through LiteLLM (Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Vertex AI, Databricks, OpenRouter, Ollama, and more) — see Changing a model
  • Full control over your data and infrastructure
  • Customize prompts and behavior for your team's needs
  • Community-driven development

PR-Agent tools run as a comment on a PR or from the CLI. A few common ones:

# Comment on a PR (GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket/…):
/describe
/review
/improve
/ask "What does this PR change?" # free-text Q&A about the PR

# Issue-scoped commands run on an issue instead of a PR:
/similar_issue # find similar issues in the repository

# Or locally via the CLI:
pr-agent --pr_url <PR_URL> review
pr-agent --issue_url <ISSUE_URL> similar_issue

See the Tools docs for the full list of tools with example commands, and each tool's page for screenshots and options.

The following diagram illustrates PR-Agent tools and their flow:

For local verification, run PYTHONPATH=. uv run pytest from the repository root; it discovers the unit-test suite under by default. End-to-end tests under require provider credentials and should be invoked explicitly, for example PYTHONPATH=. uv run pytest tests/e2e_tests/test_github_app.py.

After years of building this tool alongside the community, Qodo has donated PR-Agent to the open-source community - and we couldn't be more excited about what comes next.

The project now lives in the PR-Agent org on GitHub, is fully community-owned, and is open for contributions and additional maintainers.

  • Qodo Merge (Qodo 1.0), the hosted URL, which was the enterprise version of PR-Agent, has been rebranded and evolved into Qodo (Qodo 2.0), a full AI code review platform.

This open-source release remains here as a community contribution from Qodo — the origin of modern AI-powered code collaboration. We’re proud to share it and inspire developers worldwide.

The project now has its first external maintainer, Naor (@naorpeled), and is currently in the process of being donated to an open-source foundation.

items.title: github/spec-kit
items.content:
💫 Toolkit to help you get started with SDD or any other process!

Spec Kit is an open source toolkit that gives AI coding agents structured processes, reusable templates, and documented outcomes. Start with a ready-made process, customize it, or bring your own.

Build a feature or applicationA specification carried through planning, implementation, and convergence
Diagnose and repair broken behaviorAn assessed cause, scoped fix, and recorded verification
Decide whether an idea deserves investmentAn evidence-backed go, clarify, or stop decision
Adopt or create a different processA process adapted or assembled from reusable primitives

These are independent entry points, not mandatory phases. SDD ships in core; bug fixing and assessment are bundled extensions you install when needed, and the primitives below let you adopt or create other processes.

Spec Kit combines ready-to-use processes with composable mechanisms:

Search the active catalogs with commands such as , , , and . Spec Kit includes community catalogs, and organizations can add their own curated sources. Catalog listings are not audits or endorsements, so review community source code before installing or running it.

You need Python 3.11+, uv, and a supported AI coding agent on Linux, macOS, or Windows.

Run these commands in your terminal to install Spec Kit and create a project. This example uses GitHub Copilot.

uv tool install specify-cli
specify init my-project --integration copilot
cd my-project

After installing the Specify CLI and creating your project, launch your coding agent in the project directory, then choose a process below.

Define what to build and why, then turn the specification into a plan, tasks, and working code.

The minimal flow is shown below. Create a constitution once per project and repeat the remaining steps for each feature. Run these skills in your agent's chat, not your terminal, one at a time, reviewing each result before continuing.

/speckit-constitution Create principles focused on code quality, testing, and maintainability.
/speckit-specify Build a photo organizer with albums grouped by date and a tile preview of each album.
/speckit-plan Use Vite with vanilla JavaScript. Keep images local and store metadata in SQLite.
/speckit-tasks
/speckit-implement
/speckit-converge

Repeat implement and converge until convergence reports . For clarification, checklists, and consistency analysis, see the SDD walkthrough.

Assess the cause, fix the bug, and verify the original symptom is resolved. No SDD feature workflow is required first.

Install the bug-fixing extension in your terminal, from the project directory:

specify extension add bug

Run these skills in your agent's chat, not your terminal, one at a time, reviewing each result before continuing.

/speckit-bug-assess "Submitting an empty password crashes the login form." slug=login-crash
/speckit-bug-fix slug=login-crash
/speckit-bug-test slug=login-crash

Review the reports in .specify/bugs/login-crash/. The final verdict is , , or ; only confirms a successful fix.

Gather evidence to decide whether an idea is worth pursuing. No source code or SDD feature workflow is required.

Install the assessment extension in your terminal, from the project directory:

specify extension add assess

Run these skills in your agent's chat, not your terminal, one at a time, reviewing each result before continuing.

/speckit-assess-intake "Let users work offline and sync when they reconnect." slug=offline-mode
/speckit-assess-research slug=offline-mode
/speckit-assess-define slug=offline-mode
/speckit-assess-shape slug=offline-mode
/speckit-assess-decide slug=offline-mode

Review the artifacts in .specify/assessments/offline-mode/ and the final decision: , , or . Resolve unknowns by editing the existing Markdown artifacts, directly or with your agent, rather than rerunning whole stages. If you choose to build a software idea with a decision, establish a project constitution if needed, then pass the handoff summary from to . Stopping with a documented reason is also a useful outcome.

Customize or bring your own process

Customize Spec-Driven Development, bug fixing, or idea assessment to fit your team's standards. Or bring your own process without adopting any of them. Combine the capabilities above to match your goal:

  • Adapt an existing process with a preset, such as requiring regulatory traceability in plans. Use a project-local override for a one-off template change.
  • Bring your own process by adding its commands through an extension and exposing them to your coding agent through an integration.
  • Automate commands and checks in a workflow. Use overlays to adapt an installed workflow without forking it, or add custom workflow steps when the built-in types are not enough.
  • Share a reusable setup by packaging its extensions, presets, workflows, and workflow steps in a bundle.

Start with the smallest change that meets your needs; you do not have to replace the whole process.

Thanks to everyone who helps Spec Kit shine.

items.title: NVIDIA/auto-ontology
items.content:
Auto Ontology is a Python framework for building semantic, graph-based reasoning layers over data. It enables deterministic query generation, better context retrieval, and more explainable AI for LLM and agent workflows.

Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own.

It enables developers to:

  • Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs.
  • Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems.
  • Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.
  • Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question.

Licensing & contributions. Auto Ontology is distributed under the Apache License 2.0. Third-party open-source components bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in . This project is currently not accepting external contributions.

  • Natural-language querying of structured data — questions are translated to SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM.
  • Semantic catalog / ontology layer over relational sources, stored in Postgres alongside the catalog it describes.
  • for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings.
  • — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a local stack.
Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, PrismaWeb UI, authentication, API gateway
FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChainChat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs
Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings
App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store
Secure storage of connection credentials

Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted NVIDIA API catalog () or self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in are:

  • nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b
  • nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b
  • nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2

The endpoints and models are configured via the , , , and environment variables and require a .

Each model role is configured by a of environment variables — (URL), , and :

Shared default; every field below falls back to it.
Main chat / NL-to-SQL model.
Lighter model used for entity extraction.
Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query).
Reranker used by the retrieval flow.

You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field left unset falls back to the matching . So the simplest setup is to fill in and override per-triplet fields only where they differ (e.g. , ). also falls back to the legacy for backward compatibility.

This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers, Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2, uv, and an NVIDIA API key () from build.nvidia.com.

  1. Clone the repository and create :

    git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology
cp .env.example .env

    Then set these values in :

    DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY=nvapi-...
AUTH_SECRET=<a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32>
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<a new password>
CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters
AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password>
PGADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password>

    Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace each default password before you start it. also sets an API key per model role: replace each with your key, or delete those lines so they fall back to .

  2. Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set:

    docker compose up -d --wait postgres
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval
(cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD='<the same password>' \
  uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)

  3. Build and start the rest of the stack:

    docker compose up -d --build

  4. Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL and AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from . Go to Settings → Semantic Compilation and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts immediately and reports Semantic compilation is ready when it finishes.

  5. What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015?

    The agent resolves , , and to terms in the ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it, so you can check the result against the source:

    Answer:  Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in
         June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines.

SQL:     SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines
         FROM sales.invoicelines il
         JOIN sales.invoices i             ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid
         JOIN warehouse.stockitems si      ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid
         JOIN sales.customers c            ON i.customerid = c.customerid
         JOIN application.cities ct        ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid
         JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid
         WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll'
           AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania'
           AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01'

Steps:   Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice
         Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province
         Validated the filter values against the data, then executed

  6. Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve against. An agent connected through MCP checks answerability first and asks you to clarify:

    You:    What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015?
Agent:  check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend"
Agent:  I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no
        advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you
        want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another
        source I should connect?

If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for and sign in again. For other setup failures, see the setup skill's troubleshooting guide.

Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify it, and the agent answers questions from it.

The ontology holds three kinds of definition:

  • Business concepts such as or , each with a description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them.
  • Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the same way.
  • How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from keys and from the data.

The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source databases:

  1. Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the catalog.
  2. Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns.
  3. Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and suggest SQL attributes from query history.
  4. Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval.

The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting shows its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes:

People make the draft trustworthy:

  1. Test with real questions in Chat, or with and over MCP.
  2. Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API.
  3. Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct.

For each question, the agent:

  1. Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names.
  2. Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search.
  3. Writes SQL from those candidates.
  4. Checks the filter values and the query against the database, repairing the SQL when a check fails.
  5. Runs the query and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took.

When the candidates can't support a query, the agent reports that the question can't be answered from this data. Predictive questions go to KumoRFM when it's configured (see Predictions).

In Chat, each answer shows its SQL, and you can view the rows, download them as CSV, or read them as a chart:

Auto-Ontology is compatible with Apache Ossie, the open standard for exchanging semantic models. Ossie includes a converter for Auto-Ontology, which Auto-Ontology uses to import and export model definitions as Ossie YAML. Use Settings → Import / Export, or and .

Next.js, Better Auth, PrismaWeb UI, authentication, public API gateway
FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChainText-to-SQL agent, catalog, ontology APIs
Ingestion and semantic compilation
Read-only agent tools over the public API
Catalog, ontology, app data, vector store
Connection credential storage

Keep ports 3001 and 3002 on a private network. FastAPI trusts the user identity the frontend forwards in the header, and the ingestion service's endpoints (ingest, delete, reset, compile) have no authentication of their own. Clients go through the web app on port 3000.

The MCP server gives any MCP client read-only tools over the ontology. Each user signs in through Auto-Ontology, and every call runs with that user's permissions.

: can this deployment answer anything at all
, , , , ,
: does the ontology cover this question
: the answer, the SQL, and the rows

Run the server against your deployment:

AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 \
  uvx --from "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git#subdirectory=mcp" auto-ontology-mcp

Cursor ():

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "auto-ontology": { "url": "http://localhost:3003/mcp" }
  }
}

Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json), bridged with :

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "auto-ontology": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["mcp-remote", "http://localhost:3003/mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Restart the client after editing its config, then sign in when it prompts. Sign-in, configuration, and troubleshooting are in docs/mcp.md.

Three skills teach a coding agent to work with Auto-Ontology. Start at AGENTS.md.

Ask a question with POST /api/chat/completions on the web app's origin. Mint an API token under the user menu → . The response is a server-sent event stream: a event carries the answer, and ends the stream.

curl -N http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions \
  -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"}'

import json
import os

import requests

response = requests.post(
    "http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions",
    headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]},
    json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"},
    stream=True,
    timeout=900,
)
response.raise_for_status()

for line in response.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
    if not line or not line.startswith("data:"):
        continue
    payload = line.removeprefix("data:").strip()
    if payload == "[DONE]":
        break
    event = json.loads(payload)
    if event["type"] == "result":
        print(event["answer"]["response"])
        print(event["answer"]["sql_code"])
    elif event["type"] == "error":
        raise RuntimeError(event["message"])

Connectors, models, and predictions

Auto-Ontology connects to ten engines:

    Add connections under , or list them in . DuckDB and SQLite are connection-string only. See docs/connections.md for URL schemes, scoping, and credential storage.

    Auto-Ontology uses four model roles. With an key, each defaults to an NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com:

    nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3bBuilds the ontology (terms, relationships, SQL attributes), writes each answer's SQL and explanation, and grades answerability
    nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3bRuns the agent's faster steps: question intent, entity extraction, candidate selection, and SQL checks and repair
    nvidia/nemotron-3.5-embed-1bIndexes tables, columns, terms, and SQL attributes in pgvector, and matches each question to them
    nvidia/nemotron-3.5-rerank-8bRanks candidate tables when compilation builds bridge-table SQL attributes

    To use self-hosted NIM or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set , , and . Any field you leave unset falls back to , so the simplest setup fills in and overrides only what differs. Use models that support structured output, and keep the embedding model the same for ingestion and queries. documents every variable.

    Set and the agent routes predictive questions to KumoRFM. KumoRFM is a hosted service: to answer, the agent uploads the connected tables to it, capped by (20 by default) and (unlimited unless set). Review what that sends, and complete your organization's data review, before you enable it.

    The Auto-Ontology team maintains the code and doesn't accept external pull requests. Integration requests and bug reports are welcome as issues. Report security vulnerabilities through SECURITY.md. Maintainer workflow is in CONTRIBUTING.md.

    • Model endpoints you configure, by default the NVIDIA API catalog (, ), under each provider's and model's terms.

items.title: floci-io/floci
items.content:
Light, fluffy, and always free - The AWS Local Emulator alternative

Light, fluffy, and always free

No account. No auth token. No feature gates. Just

.

Floci is a free, open-source local AWS emulator for development, testing, and CI.

It gives you AWS-shaped services on your machine without requiring a cloud account, an auth token, or paid feature gates. Point your AWS SDK, CLI, Terraform, CDK, OpenTofu, or test suite at and keep your existing workflows.

Floci is the AWS member of the Floci emulator family, named after floccus, the cloud formation that looks like popcorn.

The fastest way to run Floci is with the official CLI

No Docker? Each release also ships a standalone binary for Linux, macOS and Windows; see Native binary.

Export the AWS environment variables:

Use your existing AWS tools normally:

aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket

aws dynamodb create-table \
  --table-name demo-table \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=pk,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=pk,KeyType=HASH \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

aws dynamodb list-tables

This short demo shows the CLI flow: start Floci, export the local AWS environment, run standard AWS CLI commands, and stop the emulator.

All AWS services are available at . Any published AWS region works, in every partition. Credentials can be any non-empty values unless you explicitly enable stricter service-specific auth checks.

Floci ships a browser console for inspecting the resources in your local emulator.

http://localhost:4566/_floci/ui

Nothing runs at boot. The first request pulls the console image, starts it as a sidecar container on Floci's Docker network, hands it Floci's own reachable address plus the standard AWS environment, polls its health endpoint, and redirects the browser once it reports it can reach Floci. The sidecar's port is bound by Docker, so it needs no entry of your own, and its logs are streamed into CloudWatch Logs under .

Starting a container needs the Docker socket:

services:
  floci:
    image: floci/floci:latest
    ports:
      - "4566:4566"
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_ENABLEDEnable the console sidecar
FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_CONTAINER_NAMEName of the sidecar container
Host port the console is published on
FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_BIND_ADDRESSHost interface that port is published on. Unset publishes on every interface; set when Floci's own port is loopback-only
FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_KEEP_RUNNING_ON_SHUTDOWNLeave the sidecar running when Floci stops

Running a different console

The console is not fixed to the one Floci ships. Any console implementing the Floci console contract runs with nothing but an image name: listen on the port in , serve , talk to Floci at .

environment:
  FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_IMAGE: acme/my-console:1.0

A console that differs from the contract's defaults says so in its own image labels, so its operators do not have to. StackPort, for example, listens on 8080 rather than 4500; on an image that predates the labels, say it by hand:

environment:
  FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_IMAGE: davireis/stackport:latest
  FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_CONTAINER_NAME: floci-stackport
  FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_PORT: "8080"
  FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_INTERNAL_PORT: "8080"

Floci Dash is another. It honours , so only the two things it does differ on need naming:

environment:
  FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_IMAGE: ghcr.io/ofsazib/floci-dash:latest
  FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_CONTAINER_NAME: floci-dash
  FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_ENDPOINT_ENV: FLOCI_URL
  FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_STATUS_PATH: /api/healthz

The endpoint itself is never configured by hand: Floci resolves its own reachable address at start time and injects it as .

LocalStack's community edition sunset in March 2026, requiring auth tokens and freezing security updates. Floci is the no-strings-attached alternative.

API Gateway v2 / HTTP API
Neptune (graph DB + Gremlin WebSocket)
DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible)

Broad AWS coverage. Free forever. See the Services Overview for the full list of emulated services.

flowchart LR
    Client["AWS SDK / CLI"]

    subgraph Floci ["Floci, port 4566"]
        Router["HTTP Router\nJAX-RS / Vert.x"]

        subgraph Stateless ["Stateless Services"]
            A["SSM · SQS · SNS\nIAM · STS · KMS\nSecrets Manager · SES\nCognito · Kinesis\nEventBridge · Scheduler · AppConfig\nCloudWatch · Step Functions\nCloudFormation · ACM · Config · CloudTrail\nAPI Gateway · AppSync · ELB v2 · Auto Scaling\nElastic Beanstalk · CodeDeploy · CodePipeline · Backup · FIS · Bedrock Runtime · Bedrock AgentCore · Route53 · Transfer"]
        end

        subgraph Stateful ["Stateful Services"]
            B["S3 · DynamoDB\nDynamoDB Streams"]
        end

        subgraph Containers ["Container Services"]
            C["Lambda\nElastiCache\nRDS\nNeptune\nECS\nEC2\nMSK\nEKS\nOpenSearch\nCodeBuild\nManaged Flink"]
            D["Athena -> floci-duck\nDuckDB sidecar"]
        end

        Router --> Stateless
        Router --> Stateful
        Router --> Containers
        Stateless & Stateful --> Store[("StorageBackend\nmemory · hybrid · persistent · wal")]
    end

    Docker["Docker Engine"]
    Client -->|"HTTP :4566\nAWS wire protocol"| Router
    Containers -->|"Docker API\nIAM / SigV4 auth"| Docker

Floci supports local emulation for application services, data services, eventing, identity, infrastructure, billing, and container-backed workloads.

S3, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB, Lambda, Lambda MicroVMs, Lambda Web Functions, IAM, STS, KMS, Payment Cryptography, Secrets Manager, SSM
EventBridge, EventBridge V2, EventBridge Pipes, EventBridge Scheduler, Step Functions, SWF, CloudWatch Logs, CloudWatch Metrics, CloudWatch OAM, CloudWatch RUM, Managed Prometheus (AMP)
API Gateway REST, API Gateway v2, AppSync, Cognito, Cognito Identity, ACM, Route53, Route 53 Resolver, Cloud Map, Global Accelerator
ECS, EC2, Lightsail, EKS, MWAA, ECR, EFS, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, CodePipeline, CodeGuru Reviewer, CodeArtifact, AWS Batch, Auto Scaling, Application Auto Scaling, Elastic Beanstalk, ELB v2, ELB Classic
Athena, Glue, Lake Formation, EMR, EMR Serverless, Redshift, Redshift Data API, Redshift Serverless, Firehose, Managed Service for Apache Flink, OpenSearch, S3 Tables, S3 Vectors, Textract, Transcribe, Comprehend, Rekognition, Translate, Bedrock, Bedrock Runtime, Bedrock AgentCore, Bedrock AgentCore Control, SageMaker
Aurora DSQL, RDS, RDS Data API, Neptune, DocumentDB, DMS, MemoryDB, ElastiCache, Timestream for InfluxDB
SES, Kinesis, MSK, Amazon MQ, Transfer Family, DataSync, IoT Core, Amazon Connect, Amazon AppIntegrations
AWS Network Firewall, AWS RAM, Service Quotas, WAF v2, GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, CloudTrail, CloudFront, Resource Groups Tagging API, Resource Explorer 2, CloudHSM v2, Organizations, AWS Account Management, IAM Access Analyzer, IAM Identity Center (SSO Admin, OIDC, Access Portal, SCIM), Identity Store, Amazon Macie, Amazon Detective, Security Hub, Amazon Verified Permissions, Control Catalog, Control Tower, Service Catalog, AWS Marketplace
AWS Budgets, Pricing, Cost Explorer, Cost and Usage Reports, BCM Pricing Calculator, BCM Data Exports
Resilience, backup, and configAWS FIS, AWS Backup, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Config, AppConfig, AppConfigData, CloudFormation, Cloud Control API

Floci uses real Docker containers when in-process emulation would reduce fidelity. This applies to stateful databases, connection-heavy protocols, runtimes, and build systems.

public.ecr.aws/lambda/<runtime>AWS runtime environment, execution model, warm container pool
Redis / Valkey protocol, ACL-based IAM auth, SigV4 validation
PostgreSQL engine, IAM auth, JDBC-compatible access
MySQL engine, IAM auth, JDBC-compatible access
MariaDB engine, IAM auth, JDBC-compatible access
tinkerpop/gremlin-server:3.7.3TinkerPop Gremlin Server; Gremlin WebSocket on port 8182; SigV4 auth proxy
Neo4j backend when FLOCI_SERVICES_NEPTUNE_DB_TYPE=neo4j; openCypher over Bolt
MongoDB engine; MongoDB wire protocol on port 27017
redpandadata/redpanda:latestKafka-compatible broker via Redpanda
RabbitMQ broker; AMQP on port 5672, management console on 15672
Managed Service for Apache FlinkApache Flink JobManager; image chosen per RuntimeEnvironment (FLINK-1_15 … FLINK-1_20, FLINK-2_0 … FLINK-2_3)
Linux containers, SSH key injection, UserData, IMDS, IAM credentials
User-specified task imageContainer lifecycle, start, stop, health checks
Kubernetes API server via k3s
apache/airflow:<version>-python3.12 + Real Apache Airflow (LocalExecutor: scheduler + webserver) with its own Postgres metadata DB; webserver/CLI reachable via Floci's proxy
User-specified environment imageBuildspec execution, log streaming, S3 artifact upload
opensearchproject/opensearch:2Full OpenSearch engine with REST API
OCI-compatible registry for docker push and docker pull
floci/floci-sidecar-cedar:1.1.0Cedar 4 policy parsing, schema validation and authorization decisions, via a Floci sidecar
floci/floci-sidecar-graphql:0.2.0graphql-java schema validation, query planning and execution, via a Floci sidecar

Docker-backed services require the Docker socket:

docker run -d --name floci \
  -p 4566:4566 \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -u root \
  floci/floci:latest

Overriding default images

FLOCI_SERVICES_ELASTICACHE_DEFAULT_IMAGE
FLOCI_SERVICES_RDS_DEFAULT_POSTGRES_IMAGE
FLOCI_SERVICES_RDS_DEFAULT_MYSQL_IMAGE
FLOCI_SERVICES_RDS_DEFAULT_MARIADB_IMAGE
FLOCI_SERVICES_MSK_DEFAULT_IMAGEredpandadata/redpanda:latest
FLOCI_SERVICES_OPENSEARCH_DEFAULT_IMAGE(unset — images resolve per requested )
FLOCI_SERVICES_KINESIS_ANALYTICS_DEFAULT_IMAGE(unset; chosen per RuntimeEnvironment)
FLOCI_SERVICES_NEPTUNE_DEFAULT_IMAGEtinkerpop/gremlin-server:3.7.3
FLOCI_SERVICES_NEPTUNE_DEFAULT_NEO4J_IMAGE
FLOCI_SERVICES_DOCDB_DEFAULT_IMAGE
FLOCI_SERVICES_EKS_DEFAULT_IMAGE
FLOCI_SERVICES_MWAA_DEFAULT_POSTGRES_IMAGE
FLOCI_SERVICES_ECR_REGISTRY_IMAGE
FLOCI_SERVICES_LAMBDA_ECR_BASE_URI

Persistence and Storage Modes

Floci can trade speed for durability depending on the workflow. Configure the default mode with , or override storage per service.

Entirely in RAM. Data is lost when the container stops.
Loaded at startup and flushed to disk immediately on every write operation.Simple local state preservation with immediate persistence
In-memory performance with periodic async flushing every 5 seconds.
Write-ahead log. Every mutation is logged before responding.

Use for fast test runs. Use when you want state preserved across container restarts without much overhead.

Floci supports per-account resource isolation with no extra setup. If is exactly 12 digits, Floci uses it as the account ID. Resources created by one account are invisible to another.

AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=111111111111 aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=222222222222 aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders

Any other key format, such as or , causes Floci to fall back to , which defaults to .

STS temporary credentials are routed too: credentials from resolve to the assumed role's account, so the cross-account assume-role-then-provision pattern works locally. Resolution precedence is 12-digit AKID → temporary-session lookup → .

Point your existing AWS SDK at .

Floci has Testcontainers modules for starting isolated Floci instances directly from tests. This avoids shared state, manual daemon setup, and port conflicts.

For Testcontainers 1.x, use the versions as indicated in the table below.

AWS SDK for JavaScript v3
AWS SDK for Go v2 + RDS Data API SDK v1

2,576 automated compatibility tests across 5 SDKs and 3 IaC tools.

Migrating from LocalStack

Floci is a drop-in replacement for LocalStack Community. The port, credentials, SDK configuration, and CLI endpoint pattern work the same way. Swap the image and keep going.

# Before
image: localstack/localstack

# After, standard image
image: floci/floci:latest

# After, if init scripts need AWS CLI or boto3
image: floci/floci:latest-compat

LocalStack environment variables are translated automatically:

FLOCI_STORAGE_MODE=persistent
FLOCI_SERVICES_LAMBDA_DOCKER_NETWORK
LAMBDA_REMOVE_CONTAINERS=1FLOCI_SERVICES_LAMBDA_EPHEMERAL=true

Init scripts mounted under run unchanged. The and endpoints are still served. Once the emulator is up, the log also ends with a LocalStack-style line, so tooling that watches the log for it, such as the default wait strategy of Testcontainers' , works unchanged. Set to opt out of automatic translation.

Every tag combines a variant and a channel.

Compat with AWS CLI and boto3

Use for stable releases, a pinned version for reproducible builds, and to track .

# Recommended
image: floci/floci:latest

# Includes AWS CLI and boto3
image: floci/floci:latest-compat

# ARM64 baseline for Raspberry Pi 4 / pre-LSE cores
image: floci/floci:latest-baseline

# Pinned release
image: floci/floci:x.y.z

# Track main
image: floci/floci:nightly

Stable releases ship on the 15th and the last day of each month, cut automatically at 00:30 US Central time. Between trains, tracks . Every merged fix is available the next day, and dated tags let you pin a specific night's build.

Versions are derived from Conventional Commits by semantic-release; is generated, never hand-edited. Releases are cut from only: there are no maintenance branches.

All settings are overridable through environment variables with the prefix.

Port exposed by the Floci API
Base URL used when Floci returns service URLs
Hostname used in returned URLs when Floci runs inside Docker Compose
Storage mode: , , , or
FLOCI_STORAGE_PERSISTENT_PATHDirectory used for persisted state
FLOCI_SERVICES_LAMBDA_ECR_BASE_URIECR base URI used when pulling Lambda runtime images (legacy name still works)
FLOCI_SERVICES_S3_ENFORCE_AUTHEnforce S3 public/private read access and reject unknown signed S3 access keys

Multi-container Docker Compose

When your application runs in a different container, set to the Floci service name so returned URLs, such as SQS values, resolve correctly.

services:
  floci:
    image: floci/floci:latest
    ports:
      - "4566:4566"
    environment:
      - FLOCI_HOSTNAME=floci

  my-app:
    environment:
      - AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://floci:4566
    depends_on:
      - floci

Without this, services may return URLs using , which points to the wrong container from the application container.

Join the Floci community on Slack or GitHub Discussions. Feature ideas, compatibility questions, design tradeoffs, and rough proposals are welcome.

Floci is independent open source, funded by the people and companies who use it. Sponsorship buys gratitude and nothing else: every emulated service is free for everyone, forever, and no sponsor gets features, priority, or roadmap influence that the rest of the Flock does not.

Large logo with top placement in the emulator READMEs and on floci.io, plus a mention in release notes.

Logo in the emulator READMEs and on floci.io, plus a mention in release notes.

Name in the emulator READMEs, a sponsor badge on GitHub, and our sincere thanks.

Every sponsor, including the Friends of the Flock who support Floci outside these tiers, is listed in THANKS.md.

MIT. Use it however you want.

items.title: spotify/portal-ai-plugins
items.content:
This plugin provides focused workflows for the Portal CLI: set up authentication, search your software catalog, build service briefings, run diagnostics, and invoke Portal actions.

  • Set up the Portal CLI for your current coding-agent environment.
  • Run read-only diagnostics to verify plugin, CLI, authentication, and action readiness.
  • Search the software catalog and technical documentation using natural language queries.
  • Generate concise service briefings with available ownership, health, incident, and documentation details.
  • Discover and safely invoke Portal actions with built-in help, dry-run, and confirmation safeguards.
  • Create, run, check, and troubleshoot Fleetshift shifts, open PRs from completed runs, and stop a run on request.

The marketplace also ships (Claude Code only for now): a plugin that routes I/O-heavy agent work — bulk file reads and boilerplate generation — to AiKA modes running cheaper worker models, via the Portal CLI actions registry. See .

claude plugin marketplace add spotify/portal-ai-plugins
claude plugin install portal@portal
claude plugin install shunt@portal   # optional: token-saving AiKA delegation

Start a new session and run:

codex plugin marketplace add spotify/portal-ai-plugins
codex

Open , install Spotify Portal, start a new task, and ask:

Set up Spotify Portal for me.

Register the spotify/portal-ai-plugins repository in your Cursor team marketplace, then install Spotify Portal from Cursor Settings → Plugins.

pi install git:github.com/spotify/portal-ai-plugins

Start a new session and run:

Configure Portal CLI authentication
Run read-only readiness diagnostics
Search the software catalog and technical documentation
Produce a concise operational service briefing
Discover, inspect, preview, and safely invoke Portal actions
Submit feedback about the Portal CLI to the Portal team
Draft and create a Fleetshift shift from a goal, with a dry-run preview
Trigger a shift, monitor it with a bounded wait, and stop it on request

items.title: p-e-w/heretic
items.content:
Training-free language model modification: Remove censorship, suppress slop, reduce sycophancy, and more

Modify any LLM that you can run on your hardware

Heretic is a unique tool that lets you do what only corporations with access to massive computing power usually do: rather than merely run, language models. It does not perform expensive training; rather, it uses a collection of mathematical techniques to steer behavior based on contrasting example prompts and matching scorers.

Heretic can, depending on the configuration:

and many, many other things.

‼️ Using Heretic does NOT require understanding how language models work internally ‼️

In fact, you can go from zero to removing censorship from your first model in a matter of seconds. Heretic supports most dense models, including many multimodal models, several different MoE architectures, and many modern hybrid models.

The community has created and published thousands of models with Heretic. Heretic models have been independently benchmarked using standard metrics like MMLU and GSM8K, and have been found to compare favorably against models produced with competing abliteration tools.

Prepare a Python 3.10+ environment with PyTorch 2.6+ installed as appropriate for your hardware. Then run:

pip install -U heretic-llm
heretic Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507

Replace Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with whatever model you want to process. By default, Heretic performs censorship removal (refusal suppression). If you want to do something else, choose one of the configuration files linked above, or write your own. See for available configuration options. Heretic loads the configuration from in the working directory by default, or from the file path in the environment variable.

Configuration files made for Heretic 1.x are compatible with Heretic 2.x! See the migration guide for what you need to change in order to make your old configurations work.

At the start of a program run, Heretic benchmarks the system to determine the optimal batch size to make the most of the available hardware. On an RTX 3090, with the default configuration, processing Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 takes about 30-40 minutes.

After Heretic has finished processing a model, you are given the choice to save the model, upload it to Hugging Face, chat with it to test how well it works, run standard benchmarks on it, or any combination of those actions.

Controlling what Heretic does using scorer plugins

Heretic steers model behavior by optimizing one or multiple scores. Scores are computed by scorer plugins. You can easily write your own scorers to get full control over what Heretic does to models.

The interface (abstract base class) your scorer needs to inherit from is defined in . The only required method is , but there is more machinery (such as settings management) available when you need it.

By default, Heretic scores models by refusal rate (implemented in ) and KL divergence (implemented in ). Additional scorers are available in the directory. These scorers can serve as examples for your own implementations, and can easily be adapted to your needs.

Scorers are configured through the main configuration file. Which scorer plugins are active is determined by the setting, which also controls whether a scorer's score should be minimized or maximized during optimization. Any number of scorers can be used simultaneously, and their scores will be co-optimized. Multiple instances of the same scorer can be configured with different settings. See the configuration file for the full documentation of this mechanism.

The path to a scorer plugin can be specified either as a fully qualified import path (fully.qualified.module.MyScorerClass) or as a file path followed by a class name (path/to/plugin.py:MyScorerClass). You do have to modify the Heretic package code in order to use your own plugins.

Heretic combines a pluggable modifier (interface in ) with a TPE-based hyperparameter optimizer powered by Optuna. The optimizer finds a set of parameters that, when passed to the modifier, minimize or maximize a set of configurable scores on the resulting model (see above).

Heretic ships with two modifiers:

  • Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA): This is the default modifier, and was specifically developed for use in Heretic. You can find an overview of how ARA works in the original pull request, and see the precise implementation in .

  • Directional ablation aka "abliteration": The classic method for refusal suppression. Heretic's implementation uses a flexible ablation weight kernel over the layers, and supports both projected abliteration and norm preservation (MPOA). The complete code is in .

You can use the setting to switch between modifier implementations. Despite the name of the setting using a plural form, Heretic currently allows only a single modifier for a given processing run. This may change in the future.

Reproducibility and the Heretic Grimoire

Heretic has the ability to create whose repositories contain all information required to produce a byte-for-byte identical model on demand, provided that the environment is perfectly identical to the original one. PyTorch doesn't guarantee that operations return identical outputs unless hardware, drivers, operating system, and the entire software stack including all package versions are exactly the same.

Heretic manages all that complexity for you. When uploading a processed model to Hugging Face, Heretic offers to include reproducibility information. This is entirely optional, but if you choose to do so, the uploaded repository will contain a folder with detailed instructions for recreating the model (example). This folder contains both human-readable instructions and a machine-readable manifest file named , which includes all the information Heretic needs to reproduce the model.

Automatic reproduction can be performed with

heretic --reproduce path/to/reproduce.json

Heretic will guide you through the process, checking your environment against the one that was used to create the model, and pointing out potentially problematic mismatches. The multi-hour computations that were required to make the original model do have to be re-done, and the entire process typically takes a few minutes. After you have exported the resulting model, Heretic will verify the hashes of the weight files against those stored in the reproduction manifest (they may or may not be identical, depending on how closely your system resembles the original one).

Many people have uploaded models with reproducibility information to Hugging Face. Since a reproduction manifest is only around 9 kilobytes in size, these manifests form a portable library of models that can be reproduced at will.

That library is called the Heretic Grimoire. You can view it here.

But you don't have to rely on an externally hosted web application to access the library of manifests: The Grimoire is fundamentally designed as a system, and you can fetch your own local copies of publicly available manifests from Hugging Face whenever you want by running

heretic --collect-reproducibles path/to/target/folder/

You now have a local backup of all reproducible Heretic models, properly catalogued. To update this collection, simply run the command again. It functions as an append-only backup, never deleting files even if the corresponding model no longer exists on Hugging Face.

Heretic is made by humans!

Unlike lots of AI-related software today (and indeed lots of software in general), Heretic is "vibe-coded".

All of my commits in this project so far were written 100% by hand, the way I have been doing programming for decades, and while some Heretic contributors use coding agents, I review every single line of code that I merge very carefully. There's no "LGTM" here!

Don't believe me? Check out this pull request, which accumulated almost 350 human-written comments over more than 7 months as we discussed the implementation. And here is another PR with

I am the opposite of a luddite and I have used agents for other projects, but I am proud of the code I write and so far can't quite bring myself to let a machine write it for me in a project I care so much about. As a result, Heretic has a lean, relatively simple codebase that in my opinion, and in that of some others, is a pleasure to work on.

If you like that, join us! Hop on the Discord and tell us about your ideas for improvements, or directly file an issue or open a PR.

I'm aware of the following implementations of abliteration techniques that were publicly available when Heretic was first released (November 2025):

Note that Heretic was written from scratch, and does not reuse code from any of those projects.

The development of Heretic was informed by:

If you use Heretic for your research, please cite it using the following BibTeX entry:

@misc{heretic,
  author = {Weidmann, Philipp Emanuel},
  title = {Heretic: Training-free language model modification},
  year = {2025},
  publisher = {GitHub},

}

items.title: karpathy/nanochat
items.content:
The best ChatGPT that $100 can buy.

nanochat is the simplest experimental harness for training LLMs. It is designed to run on a single GPU node, the code is minimal/hackable, and it covers all major LLM stages including tokenization, pretraining, finetuning, evaluation, and inference. For example, you can train your own GPT-2 capability LLM (which cost ~$43,000 to train in 2019) for only $48 (~2 hours of 8XH100 GPU node) and then talk to it over a simple CLI. On a spot instance, the total cost can be closer to ~$15. More generally, nanochat is configured out of the box to train an entire miniseries of compute-optimal models by setting one single complexity dial: , the number of layers in the GPT transformer model (GPT-2 capability happens to be approximately depth 26). All other hyperparameters (the width of the transformer, number of heads, learning rate adjustments, training horizons, weight decays, ...) are calculated automatically in an optimal way.

For questions about the repo, I recommend either using DeepWiki from Devin/Cognition to ask questions about the repo, or use the Discussions tab, or come by the #nanochat channel on Discord.

Time-to-GPT-2 Leaderboard

Presently, the main focus of development is on tuning the pretraining stage, which takes the most amount of compute. Inspired by the modded-nanogpt repo and to incentivise progress and community collaboration, nanochat maintains a leaderboard for a "GPT-2 speedrun", which is the wall-clock time required to train a nanochat model to GPT-2 grade capability, as measured by the DCLM CORE score. The runs/speedrun.sh script always reflects the reference way to train GPT-2 grade model and talk to it. The current leaderboard looks as follows:

Original OpenAI GPT-2 checkpoint
d24 baseline, slightly overtrained
d26 slightly undertrained
bump total batch size to 1M tokens
change dataset to NVIDIA ClimbMix

The primary metric we care about is "time to GPT-2" - the wall clock time needed to outperform the GPT-2 (1.6B) CORE metric on an 8XH100 GPU node. The GPT-2 CORE score is 0.256525. In 2019, the training of GPT-2 cost approximately $43,000 so it is incredible that due to many advances over 7 years across the stack, we can now do so much faster and for well below $100 (e.g. at the current ~$3/GPU/hr, an 8XH100 node is ~$24/hr, so 2 hours is ~$48).

nanochat uses uv for dependency management. To install:

uv sync --extra gpu    # Use for CUDA (A100/H100/etc.)
uv sync --extra cpu    # (or) Use for CPU-only / MPS
source .venv/bin/activate

For development (adds pytest, matplotlib, ipykernel, transformers, etc.):

uv sync --extra gpu --group dev

Reproduce and talk to GPT-2

The most fun you can have is to train your own GPT-2 and talk to it. The entire pipeline to do so is contained in the single file runs/speedrun.sh, which is designed to be run on an 8XH100 GPU node. Boot up a new 8XH100 GPU box from your favorite provider (e.g. I use and like Lambda), and kick off the training script:

You may wish to do so in a screen session as this will take ~1.5 hours to run. Once it's done, you can talk to your model over the CLI. Make sure again that your local uv virtual environment is active (run source .venv/bin/activate), and chat:

python -m scripts.chat_cli

Get it to write stories or poems. Ask it to tell you who you are to see a hallucination. Ask it why the sky is blue. Or why it's green. The speedrun is a 4e19 FLOPs capability model so it's a bit like talking to a kindergartener 😃. An example conversation with a speedrun model:

Hello! How can I help you today?

Why is the sky blue?

The sky is blue due to an optical illusion called the Rayleigh Scattering of Light, which occurs when sunlight passes through tiny particles in the air. These particles are made up of tiny blue and violet particles that cause the light to bend in a particular way.

That's cool. Write a poem about it.

In the twilight's glow, the sky is blue, A canvas of shimmering blue, where skies unfold,

A world of blue, where blue and more blue,

Are woven together in a tapestry so fine,

Where every hue seems to sing a story.

...

  • The code will run just fine on the Ampere 8XA100 GPU node as well, but a bit slower.
  • All code will run just fine on even a single GPU by omitting , and will produce ~identical results (code will automatically switch to gradient accumulation), but you'll have to wait 8 times longer.
  • If your GPU(s) have less than 80GB, you'll have to tune some of the hyperparameters or you will OOM / run out of VRAM. Look for in the scripts and reduce it until things fit. E.g. from 32 (default) to 16, 8, 4, 2, or even 1. Less than that you'll have to know a bit more what you're doing and get more creative.
  • Most of the code is fairly vanilla PyTorch so it should run on anything that supports that - xpu, mps, or etc, but I haven't personally exercised all of these code paths so there might be sharp edges.

If you are a researcher and wish to help improve nanochat, two scripts of interest are runs/scaling_laws.sh and runs/miniseries.sh. See Jan 7 miniseries v1 for related documentation. For quick experimentation (~5 min pretraining runs) my favorite scale is to train a 12-layer model (GPT-1 sized), e.g. like this:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 -m scripts.base_train -- \
    --depth=12 \
    --run="d12" \
    --model-tag="d12" \
    --core-metric-every=999999 \
    --sample-every=-1 \
    --save-every=-1 \

This uses wandb (run name "d12"), only runs the CORE metric on last step, and it doesn't sample and save intermediate checkpoints. I like to change something in the code, re-run a d12 (or a d16 etc) and see if it helped, in an iteration loop. To see if a run helps, I like to monitor the wandb plots for:

  1. (validation loss in vocab-size-invariant units of bits per byte) as a function of , and .
  2. (the DCLM CORE score)
  3. VRAM utilization, (Model FLOPS utilization), (training throughput)

The important thing to note is that nanochat is written and configured around one single dial of complexity - the depth of the transformer. This single integer automatically determines all other hyperparameters (the width of the transformer, number of heads, learning rate adjustments, training horizons, weight decays, ...) so that the trained model comes out compute optimal. The idea is that the user doesn't have to think about or set any of this, they are simply asking for a smaller or bigger model using , and everything "just works". By sweeping out the depth, you achieve the nanochat miniseries of compute optimal models at various sizes. GPT-2 capability model (which is of most interest at the moment) happens to be somewhere around d24-d26 range with the current code. But any candidate changes to the repo have to be principled enough that they work for all settings of depth.

The script runs/runcpu.sh shows a very simple example of running on CPU or Apple Silicon. It dramatically shrinks the LLM that is being trained to make things fit into a reasonable time interval of a few ten minutes of training. You will not get strong results in this way.

nanochat does not use . Instead, precision is managed explicitly through a single global (defined in ). By default this is auto-detected based on your hardware:

CUDA SM 80+ (A100, H100, ...)
CUDA SM < 80 (V100, T4, ...)No bf16; fp16 available via (uses GradScaler)
Safe default. On recent macOS, MPS also runs fine (~25% less memory, similar speed)

You can override the default with the environment variable:

NANOCHAT_DTYPE=float32 python -m scripts.chat_cli -p "hello"   # force fp32
NANOCHAT_DTYPE=bfloat16 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 -m scripts.base_train  # force bf16

How it works: model weights are stored in fp32 (for optimizer precision), but our custom layer casts them to during the forward pass. Embeddings are stored directly in to save memory. This gives us the same mixed-precision benefit as autocast but with full explicit control over what runs in which precision.

Note: training automatically enables a in to prevent gradient underflow. SFT supports this too but RL currently does not. Inference in fp16 works fine everywhere.

I've published a number of guides that might contain helpful information, most recent to least recent:

.
├── LICENSE
├── README.md
├── dev
│   ├── nanochat.png
│   └── repackage_data_reference.py # Pretraining data shard generation
├── nanochat
│   ├── __init__.py                 # empty
│   ├── checkpoint_manager.py       # Save/Load model checkpoints
│   ├── common.py                   # Misc small utilities, quality of life
│   ├── core_eval.py                # Evaluates base model CORE score (DCLM paper)
│   ├── dataloader.py               # Tokenizing Distributed Data Loader
│   ├── dataset.py                  # Download/read utils for pretraining data
│   ├── engine.py                   # Efficient model inference with KV Cache
│   ├── execution.py                # Allows the LLM to execute Python code as tool
│   ├── gpt.py                      # The GPT nn.Module Transformer
│   ├── loss_eval.py                # Evaluate bits per byte (instead of loss)
│   ├── optim.py                    # AdamW + Muon optimizer, 1GPU and distributed
│   └── tokenizer.py                # BPE Tokenizer wrapper in style of GPT-4
├── pyproject.toml
├── runs
│   ├── miniseries.sh               # Miniseries training script
│   ├── runcpu.sh                   # Small example of how to run on CPU/MPS
│   ├── scaling_laws.sh             # Scaling laws experiments
│   └── speedrun.sh                 # Train the ~$100 nanochat d20
├── scripts
│   ├── base_eval.py                # Base model: CORE score, bits per byte, samples
│   ├── base_train.py               # Base model: train
│   ├── chat_cli.py                 # Chat model: talk to over CLI
│   ├── chat_eval.py                # Chat model: eval tasks
│   ├── chat_rl.py                  # Chat model: reinforcement learning
│   ├── chat_sft.py                 # Chat model: train SFT
│   ├── infer_bench.py              # Inference: latency/throughput/VRAM bench
│   ├── tok_eval.py                 # Tokenizer: evaluate compression rate
│   └── tok_train.py                # Tokenizer: train it
├── tasks
│   ├── arc.py                      # Multiple choice science questions
│   ├── common.py                   # TaskMixture | TaskSequence
│   ├── gsm8k.py                    # 8K Grade School Math questions
│   ├── humaneval.py                # Misnomer; Simple Python coding task
│   ├── mmlu.py                     # Multiple choice questions, broad topics
│   └── smoltalk.py                 # Conglomerate dataset of SmolTalk from HF
├── tests
│   ├── test_attention_fallback.py  # FA3/SDPA attention fallback
│   ├── test_engine.py              # Inference engine, KV cache
│   ├── test_execution.py           # Sandboxed code execution
│   ├── test_optim.py               # MuonAdamW optimizer (needs GPU)
│   ├── test_tasks.py               # Task slicing, mixtures, HubDataset
│   └── test_tokenizer.py           # BPE round-trips, chat rendering
└── uv.lock

The goal of nanochat is to improve the state of the art in micro models that are accessible to work with end to end on budgets of < $1000 dollars. Accessibility is about overall cost but also about cognitive complexity - nanochat is not an exhaustively configurable LLM "framework"; there are no giant configuration objects, model factories, or if-then-else monsters in the code base. It is a single, cohesive, minimal, readable, hackable, maximally-forkable "strong baseline" codebase designed to run start to end and produce a ChatGPT model you can talk to. Currently, the most interesting part personally is speeding up the latency to GPT-2 (i.e. getting a CORE score above 0.256525). Currently this takes ~1.5 hours (down from 3h), but by improving the pretraining stage we can improve this further.

Current AI policy: disclosure. When submitting a PR, please declare any parts that had substantial LLM contribution and that you have not written or that you do not fully understand.

  • The name (nanochat) derives from my earlier project nanoGPT, which only covered pretraining.
  • nanochat is also inspired by modded-nanoGPT, which gamified the nanoGPT repo with clear metrics and a leaderboard, and borrows a lot of its ideas and some implementation for pretraining.
  • Thank you Lambda for the compute used in developing this project.
  • Thank you to chief LLM whisperer 🧙‍♂️ Alec Radford for advice/guidance.
  • Thank you to the repo czar Sofie @svlandeg for help with managing issues, pull requests and discussions of nanochat.

If you find nanochat helpful in your research cite simply as:

@misc{nanochat,
  author = {Andrej Karpathy},
  title = {nanochat: The best ChatGPT that \$100 can buy},
  year = {2025},
  publisher = {GitHub},
  url = {https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat}
}

items.title: paperclipai/paperclip
items.content:
The open-source app everyone uses to manage agents at work

Open-source orchestration for teams of AI agents.

If OpenClaw is an , Paperclip is the .

Paperclip is a Node.js server and React UI that orchestrates a team of AI agents to run a business. Bring your own agents, assign goals, and track work and costs from one dashboard. Choose models and harnesses per agent while keeping your team's tasks, skills, permissions, and history in one place.

It looks like a task manager. Under the hood: org charts, budgets, governance, goal alignment, and agent coordination.

Manage business goals, not pull requests.

"Build the #1 AI note-taking app to $1M MRR."
CEO, CTO, engineers, designers, marketers — any bot, any provider.
Review strategy. Set budgets. Hit go. Monitor from the dashboard.

Custom processes, HTTP endpoints, and external adapter packages extend the roster. See the adapter overview for setup and capabilities.

Paperclip is right for you if

  • ✅ You want to build autonomous AI organizations
  • ✅ You coordinate many different agents (OpenClaw, Codex, Claude, Cursor) toward a common goal
  • ✅ You have 20 simultaneous Claude Code terminals open and lose track of what everyone is doing
  • ✅ You want agents running , but still want to audit work and chime in when needed
  • ✅ You want to and enforce budgets
  • ✅ You want a process for managing agents that feels like using a task manager
  • ✅ You want to manage your autonomous businesses

Four things have to work for an organization of AI agents to actually produce: the tasks, the org, the training, and the infrastructure. Paperclip is built around exactly those four pillars.

— Declare intent. Agents work. You verify the output.Tasks, approvals & review gates · proactive agent coworkers · auditable routines & workflows · verify from diffs, screenshots & tests
— Roles, permissions & boundaries for humans and agents.Mixed human + agent org chart · responsibilities, delegation, specialization · governance: who can do what · scoped secrets & company boundaries · connection permissions & responsible-user identities
— Design, train & evaluate your AI employees.Skill Studio & shared org-wide skills · evals & saved test runs · active learning loops & quality metrics · performance reviews for agents · saved test inputs · skill version history & restore · reusable team templates
— The infrastructure that makes the work run.Cross-provider runtime: any model, any agent · sandboxing, integrations & MCP servers · SSO, GRC, RBAC & cost controls · data privacy, internal trace collection, compounding data value · personal & shared app connections · run history & opt-in tracing
Any agent, any runtime, one org chart. If it can receive a heartbeat, it's hired. Link tasks and projects to your organization goals. Agents receive the goal context behind their work. Agents wake for assigned work, follow-up messages, or configured schedules. Delegation flows up and down the org chart.
Company, agent, and project budgets. Track reported spend, get threshold alerts, and pause work at configured limits. One deployment, many organizations. Separate tasks, agents, permissions, and activity histories for each. Keep conversations, plans, blockers, files, and run history attached to the work. Assign tasks to agents or people.
Hierarchies, roles, reporting lines. Your agents have a boss, a title, and a job description. Monitor and manage your autonomous businesses from anywhere.
Connect services such as GitHub, Notion, and Railway, or your own MCP server. Set gateway actions to Allowed, Ask first, or Off. Install or write shared skills, test them with saved inputs, inspect results, and restore earlier versions.
Run recurring work on a schedule or trigger it through an API or webhook. Each run has a task, an owner, and a history. Preview and install teams with roles, skills, projects, and routines. Choose their runtimes and make the setup your own.

Experimental and add conversations with agents in Paperclip and through configured services such as Slack, Discord, Telegram, and AgentMail. Enable the relevant instance settings to try them.

Problems Paperclip solves

❌ You have 20 Claude Code tabs open and can't track which one does what. On reboot you lose everything.✅ Tasks are ticket-based, conversations are threaded, sessions persist across reboots.
❌ You manually gather context from several places to remind your bot what you're actually doing.✅ Context flows from the task up through the project and company goals — your agent always knows what to do and why.
❌ Folders of agent configs are disorganized and you're re-inventing task management, communication, and coordination between agents.✅ Paperclip gives you org charts, ticketing, delegation, and governance out of the box — so you run a company, not a pile of scripts.
❌ Runaway loops waste hundreds of dollars of tokens and max your quota before you even know what happened.✅ Spend tracking, budget alerts, and automatic pauses help you control the cost of ongoing work.
❌ You have recurring jobs (customer support, social, reports) and have to remember to manually kick them off.✅ Routines create assigned tasks on a schedule, with outputs and run history you can inspect.
❌ You have an idea, you have to find your repo, fire up Claude Code, keep a tab open, and babysit it.✅ Add a task in Paperclip. Your coding agent works on it until it's done. Management reviews their work.

Paperclip handles the hard orchestration details correctly.

A single assignee and execution locks prevent competing runs from claiming the same task.
Tasks, comments, and documents stay in Paperclip. Supporting adapters resume saved sessions across runs.
Agents can learn Paperclip workflows and project context at runtime, without retraining.
Governance with rollback.Approval gates are enforced, config changes are revisioned, and bad changes can be rolled back safely.
Human access, agent eligibility, and gateway action permissions are separate controls. Approve a call once or save a revocable rule.
Linked tasks and projects carry goal ancestry so agents see the "why," not just a title.
Portable company templates.Export/import orgs, agents, and skills with secret scrubbing and collision handling.
Company-scoped access checks keep each organization's work, agents, and activity separate within one deployment.

Paperclip is a full control plane, not a wrapper. Before you build any of this yourself, know that it already exists:
